AI.method: TimeClaw integrates three components: (1) executable temporal tools for grounded/auditable analysis, (2) experience-driven capability evolution for creating reusable analytical routines, and (3) episodic multimodal memory for retrieving relevant reasoning traces — all enabling harnessed open-ended temporal reasoning.
AI.result: Extensive evaluation on multiple benchmarks across energy, finance, weather, traffic, and other real-world domains demonstrates improved performance of TimeClaw.
AI.conclusion: TimeClaw effectively bridges the gap between generalist LLM agents and structured temporal data, enabling contextualized temporal reasoning for real-world time series workflows.

title: Accelerating and Scaling MPC-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Humanoid Locomotion and Manipulation
summary: In humanoid motion control, model predictive control (MPC) offers physically grounded prediction and constraint handling, while reinforcement learning (RL) enables robust whole-body skills through large-scale simulation. However, using MPC inside RL often requires time-consuming problem construction or excessive training overhead, making such frameworks difficult to justify in practice. This work studies efficient training-time MPC guidance for humanoid locomotion and manipulation, termed MPC-RL. We introduce a centroidal-dynamics MPC reward formulation that leverages guidance from MPC trajectories in training time. To make this practical in massively parallel RL, we develop $π^n$MPC, a parallel-in-horizon and construction-free batched GPU MPC solver that operates directly on time-varying dynamics to avoid high memory usage and pre-compilation. Through a variety of comparative studies and hardware validations, we have found that MPC-RL achieves superior performance in locomotion and manipulation skills. The code base is available at https://github.com/junhengl/mpc-rl.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MPC-RL, a framework that uses efficient, parallelized centroidal-dynamics MPC guidance during RL training to improve humanoid locomotion and manipulation, enabled by a novel batched GPU MPC solver ($\pi^n$MPC) that avoids high memory usage and pre-compilation.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches combining MPC with RL suffer from time-consuming problem construction or excessive training overhead, making them impractical. The authors seek an efficient way to leverage MPC's physically grounded predictions as guidance during RL training without these drawbacks.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) a centroidal-dynamics MPC reward formulation that uses MPC trajectories as guidance during RL training, and (2) $\pi^n$MPC, a parallel-in-horizon, construction-free batched GPU MPC solver that operates on time-varying dynamics to eliminate high memory usage and pre-compilation, enabling massively parallel RL integration.
AI.result: Through comparative studies and hardware validations, MPC-RL achieves superior performance in both locomotion and manipulation skills for humanoid robots.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MPC-RL framework successfully combines the benefits of MPC (physical grounding, constraint handling) with RL (robust whole-body skills via large-scale simulation) in an efficient and practical manner, validated on real hardware, with open-source code.

title: Agents' Last Exam
summary: Recent AI systems have achieved strong results on a wide range of benchmarks, yet these gains have not translated into economically meaningful deployment across many professional domains. We argue that this gap is largely an evaluation problem: widely used benchmarks lack sustained performance measurement on real and economically valuable workflows. This paper introduces Agents' Last Exam (ALE), a benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents on long-horizon, economically valuable, real-world tasks with verifiable outcomes. Developed in collaboration with 250+ industry experts, ALE covers non-physical industries defined with reference to O*NET / SOC 2018 (the U.S. federal occupational taxonomy). It is organized around a task taxonomy with 55 subfields grouped into 13 industry clusters covering 1K+ tasks. Current results show that the hardest tier remains far from saturated: across mainstream harness and backbone configurations, the average full pass rate is 2.6%. ALE is designed as a living benchmark: its task pool grows continuously as new workflows and industries are onboarded. More broadly, ALE is intended not merely as another leaderboard, but as an instrument for closing the gap between benchmark success and GDP-relevant impact.

AI.tldr: ALE is a living benchmark of 1K+ real-world tasks across 13 industry clusters, where the hardest tier achieves only 2.6% average pass rate, designed to bridge the gap between benchmark performance and economically meaningful AI deployment.
AI.motivation: Current AI benchmarks show strong results but fail to translate into economically meaningful real-world deployment; this gap is largely an evaluation problem due to lack of sustained measurement on real, economically valuable workflows.
AI.method: Developed with 250+ industry experts, organized by O*NET/SOC 2018 taxonomy into 13 industry clusters and 55 subfields covering 1K+ tasks; tasks are long-horizon, real-world, with verifiable outcomes; designed as a living benchmark with continuous task pool growth.
AI.result: Across mainstream harness and backbone configurations, the hardest tier achieves an average full pass rate of only 2.6%, indicating the benchmark remains far from saturated.
AI.conclusion: ALE is intended as an instrument for closing the gap between benchmark success and GDP-relevant impact, not merely another leaderboard.

title: DexFuture: Hierarchical Future-State Visuomotor Targeting for Bimanual Dexterous Tool Use
summary: Bimanual dexterous tool use remains challenging for robots due to high-dimensional hand configurations and complex hand-tool-object dynamics and contact. Most existing control policies depend on future configuration references provided from demonstrations, while future action-conditioned world models require slow online planning over high-dimensional action sequences. A significant challenge is generating a dynamically consistent future reference trajectory without relying on privileged states from demonstrations or slow counterfactual planning. We propose DexFuture, a hierarchical system that couples a high-level Future-State Visuomotor Target Predictor with a low-level Target-Conditioned Structured Dexterous Policy. Conditioned on egocentric RGB, proprioceptive and geometric history, the high-level predictor constructs structured hand-tool-object visuomotor embeddings and uses a horizon-conditioned transformer to generate a multi-step future target trajectory. Then, the low-level policy tracks them with a target-conditioned per-link transformer. This hierarchy decouples coarse future reference generation from fine-grained action control, and slow long-horizon semantic prediction from high-frequency execution. On OakInk2 bimanual tool-use tasks, DexFuture achieves 90% of the privileged-oracle performance, compared to 7% for a no-reference policy. DexFuture operates at 60 Hz, approximately 250 times faster than DexWM-style Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) planning with a future action-conditioned world model.

AI.tldr: DexFuture is a hierarchical system for bimanual dexterous tool use that couples a high-level Future-State Visuomotor Target Predictor (horizon-conditioned transformer) with a low-level Target-Conditioned Structured Dexterous Policy (per-link transformer), achieving 90% of privileged-oracle performance without demonstrations and operating 250x faster than CEM planning.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for bimanual dexterous manipulation either rely on privileged state references from demonstrations (limiting generalization) or require slow online planning over high-dimensional action sequences via world models (limiting speed). A dynamically consistent future reference trajectory without demonstrations or slow counterfactual planning is needed.
AI.method: A two-level hierarchy: (1) High-level Future-State Visuomotor Target Predictor uses egocentric RGB, proprioceptive, and geometric history with a horizon-conditioned transformer to generate multi-step future target trajectories via structured hand-tool-object visuomotor embeddings. (2) Low-level Target-Conditioned Structured Dexterous Policy uses a per-link transformer to track these targets, decoupling coarse future generation from fine-grained control and slow semantic prediction from high-frequency execution.
AI.result: On OakInk2 bimanual tool-use tasks, DexFuture achieves 90% of privileged-oracle performance (vs 7% for no-reference policy). Operates at 60 Hz, approximately 250x faster than DexWM-style CEM planning with action-conditioned world models.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical decomposition effectively addresses the challenge of generating dynamic future references without privileged information, enabling both high performance and real-time operation for bimanual dexterous tool use.

title: Mutation Without Variation: Convergence Dynamics in LLM-Driven Program Evolution
comment: Accepted to the Genetic and Evolutionary Computation Conference (GECCO '26) Workshop on Large Language Models for and with Evolutionary Computation
summary: When an LLM repeatedly mutates a program, does it explore new forms or circle back to the same ones? We study this question by analyzing LLM-driven mutation chains in the absence of selection pressure within a domain-specific language, varying prompt design, model family, and stochastic replication. We find that LLM-based mutation consistently converges toward restricted attractor regions in program space. Convergence is especially severe at the structural level: in 87% of chains, over 93% of mutations revisit a previously seen structural form, with most variation confined to terminal substitutions within recurring templates. Cycle analysis reveals short cycles and self-loops dominating the transition structure. The rate of convergence varies with prompt wording and model choice, but the phenomenon is robust across conditions. A classical GP subtree mutation operator does not exhibit comparable convergence, suggesting that the effect is intrinsic to the LLM mutation pipeline. These findings reveal a tension at the heart of LLM-driven program evolution: the same capabilities that enable semantics-aware program transformation also carry a systematic bias toward structural homogeneity that must be accounted for if such systems are to sustain open-ended exploration. Source code is available at https://github.com/can-gurkan/lmca.

AI.tldr: LLM-driven program mutation converges toward restricted attractor regions in program space, with 87% of chains having over 93% of mutations revisiting previously seen structural forms, dominated by short cycles and self-loops, unlike classical GP subtree mutation.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether LLM-based program mutation in the absence of selection pressure explores novel program forms or converges to repetitive structures, revealing the intrinsic bias of LLM-driven mutation pipelines.
AI.method: Analyzed LLM-driven mutation chains in a domain-specific language without selection pressure, varying prompt design, model family, and stochastic replication; compared with classical GP subtree mutation operator.
AI.result: LLM mutation consistently converges to attractor regions; 87% of chains show over 93% of mutations revisiting prior structural forms; convergence robust across conditions; GP subtree mutation does not exhibit comparable convergence.
AI.conclusion: LLMs' semantics-aware mutation capability comes with a systematic bias toward structural homogeneity, posing a tension for sustaining open-ended program evolution.

title: PiL-World: A Chunk-Wise World Model for VLA Policy-in-the-Loop Evaluation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies operate in a closed loop in real-world robot tasks: a robot observes the scene, executes an action chunk, and conditions its next decision on the resulting observation. However, most existing world models for robot action evaluation are limited to open-loop prediction along pre-collected action trajectories. This prevents them from supporting closed-loop VLA evaluation, where each action chunk must be conditioned on the observation generated by the previous execution. To address this gap, we propose PiL-World, a chunk-wise world model designed for policy-in-the-loop VLA evaluation. Given the current observation and the action trajectory rolled out by a VLA policy, PiL-World generates multi-view future observations that are consistent with the VLA rollout and match the image inputs required by the policy. By alternating between VLA inference and world-model prediction, PiL-World enables closed-loop evaluation without real robot execution at every step. To improve rollout fidelity, PiL-World conditions video generation on action-derived visual control from head-view robot motion and latent histories that encode task execution context, while jointly predicting complementary multi-view observations. Beyond successful teleoperated demonstrations, it also learns from failed execution trajectories, helping the imagined rollouts better match the distribution of real policy executions. We evaluate PiL-World on three real dual-arm manipulation tasks. PiL-World generates imagined rollouts that are highly consistent with real robot executions. More importantly, compared with the baseline, it reduces the error between VLA success rates measured in real-world rollouts and those estimated through closed-loop world-model evaluation from 63.2% to 12.0%.

AI.tldr: PiL-World is a chunk-wise world model for closed-loop VLA policy evaluation, generating multi-view future observations conditioned on policy rollouts without real robot execution, reducing evaluation error from 63.2% to 12.0%.
AI.motivation: Existing world models for robot action evaluation are limited to open-loop prediction along pre-collected trajectories, unable to support closed-loop VLA evaluation where actions must be conditioned on observations from previous executions.
AI.method: PiL-World alternates between VLA inference and world-model prediction in a closed loop; conditions video generation on action-derived visual control from head-view robot motion and latent histories encoding task context; jointly predicts complementary multi-view observations; and learns from both successful and failed execution trajectories.
AI.result: On three real dual-arm manipulation tasks, PiL-World generates rollouts highly consistent with real executions, reducing the error between VLA success rates measured in real-world and those estimated via closed-loop evaluation from 63.2% to 12.0%.
AI.conclusion: PiL-World enables effective closed-loop VLA evaluation without real robot execution at every step, significantly improving evaluation fidelity compared to baselines.

title: A Motivational Architecture for Conversational AGI
summary: Motivational architectures in cognitive AI have largely been designed for physical agents regulating bodily needs. Conversational agents operate in a different regime: their sensorimotor loop is linguistic, their environment is a user's evolving mental state, and their consequential actions are speech acts, tool invocations, and strategic silences. This paper proposes a conversational reinterpretation of the OpenPsi motivational lineage, coupled to MetaMo's higher-level motivational scaffold, for agents built on a modular execution substrate. Homeostasis is recast in dialogue-native terms: the agent regulates competence, uncertainty reduction, affiliation, affinity, legitimacy, nurturing, and aesthetic coherence rather than bodily deficits. We propose three contributions: a ten-stage motivational processing pipeline that architecturally separates cognitive modulation from situational appraisal; a dual decision strategy blending urgency-driven fast response with deliberative multi-goal optimization; and an architecturally useful distinction between pre-action feelings and post-action emotions as functionally different forms of affect. We specialize the framework to two example agents -- CompanionAgent and ResearchAgent -- and sketch its extension to social robotics and domain-generic human-level AGI.

AI.tldr: This paper reinterprets the OpenPsi motivational architecture for conversational agents, replacing bodily homeostasis with dialogue-native regulation (competence, uncertainty, affiliation, etc.), and proposes a ten-stage motivational pipeline, a dual decision strategy (urgency vs. deliberation), and a functional distinction between pre-action feelings and post-action emotions, demonstrated through CompanionAgent and ResearchAgent examples.
AI.motivation: Existing motivational architectures in cognitive AI are designed for physical agents with bodily needs, but conversational agents operate in a fundamentally different regime where the sensorimotor loop is linguistic, the environment is the user's mental state, and actions are speech acts, tool invocations, or silences. A domain-appropriate motivational framework is needed.
AI.method: The authors propose a conversational reinterpretation of the OpenPsi motivational lineage coupled with MetaMo's higher-level motivational scaffold, featuring: (1) a ten-stage motivational processing pipeline that separates cognitive modulation from situational appraisal; (2) a dual decision strategy blending urgency-driven fast response with deliberative multi-goal optimization; and (3) an architectural distinction between pre-action feelings and post-action emotions as functionally different forms of affect. Homeostasis is recast in dialogue-native terms (competence, uncertainty reduction, affiliation, affinity, legitimacy, nurturing, aesthetic coherence).
AI.result: Two specialized agent instantiations are presented: CompanionAgent and ResearchAgent. The framework's extension to social robotics and domain-generic human-level AGI is sketched.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a principled motivational architecture tailored to conversational agents, with potential applicability beyond pure dialogue to social robotics and general AGI systems.

title: Visuotactile and Explicitly Force-Controlled Robotic Ultrasound for Abdominal Volumetric Reconstruction
summary: In this paper, we present a robotic ultrasound acquisition system that integrates stereo vision, touch-based feedback, and expert-informed strategies to perform autonomous and adaptive abdominal scans. The system records freehand motion and force data from expert radiologists, creating a framework to capture transducer motion, applied forces, and anatomical scanning strategies. This expert data is replayed to replicate characteristic scans with the robot, forming a foundation for further autonomous capabilities. Using stereo vision, the system generates three-dimensional topography maps of the patient's abdomen, which are refined through stiffness measurements at key points to delineate the rib cage boundary. These combined techniques enable the robot to execute two distinct scanning paths: an upward-angled sweep beneath the rib cage to visualize structures near the upper abdomen and a perpendicular sweep across soft tissue regions. A compliant, torque-controlled seven degree-of-freedom robotic manipulator is controlled to maintain consistent probe contact through closed-loop force control over the varied anatomical surfaces. Physical experiments demonstrate that the system achieves high-quality imaging comparable to expert scans while dynamically adapting to patient-specific topographies. Furthermore, the robotic system surpasses expert capabilities by enabling three-dimensional volume acquisition, which enhances diagnostic potential and provides volumetric data for advanced analyses. This work highlights the integration of expert knowledge into autonomous robotic systems and underscores the potential of combining perception-based autonomy with physical reasoning for enhanced diagnostic performance.

AI.tldr: A robotic ultrasound system uses stereo vision, force sensing, and expert data replication to autonomously scan abdomens, producing expert-quality images and enabling 3D volume acquisition.
AI.motivation: To create an autonomous robotic ultrasound system that replicates expert radiologists' scanning techniques, adapts to patient-specific anatomies, and overcomes limitations of freehand scanning (e.g., lack of 3D volume data).
AI.method: Expert freehand motion/force data is recorded and replayed. Stereo vision generates 3D abdominal topography maps refined by stiffness measurements to locate the rib cage. A torque-controlled 7-DOF manipulator executes two scan paths (upward-angled sweep under ribs, perpendicular sweep over soft tissue) with closed-loop force control.
AI.result: The system achieves imaging quality comparable to expert scans while dynamically adapting to patient-specific topographies, and surpasses human capability by enabling 3D volume acquisition.
AI.conclusion: Integrating expert knowledge with perception-based autonomy and physical reasoning enhances diagnostic performance, highlighting the potential of autonomous robotic ultrasound for advanced clinical analysis.

title: Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of U.S. Hyperscale Data Centers
summary: The rapid proliferation of hyperscale data centers (HDCs) in the US, mainly driven by the adoption of artificial intelligence, has raised concerns about this industry's environmental footprint. We compiled facility-level information on 403 US hyperscale data centers operating between May 2024 and April 2025 and estimated their electricity consumption, electricity sources, and attributable CO2 emissions. Across different facility-load scenarios, these HDCs consumed approximately 68-99 TWh of electricity and were associated with about 37-54 million metric tons of CO2. Under the central scenario, HDC electricity demand corresponded to approximately 1.8% of total US electricity consumption, with roughly 54% of attributed generation supplied by fossil-fuel sources. The HDC electricity-weighted average carbon intensity was approximately 545 gCO2/kWh, about 48% above the contemporaneous US national grid-average carbon intensity of 370 gCO2/kWh. Our approach provides an attributional tool for assessing the environmental footprint of hyperscale data centers using the most recent EPA eGRID plant-level data.

AI.tldr: This study analyzed 403 US hyperscale data centers (May 2024–April 2025), finding they consumed 68–99 TWh electricity (~1.8% of US total) and emitted 37–54 Mt CO2, with a carbon intensity (545 gCO2/kWh) ~48% higher than the US grid average (370 gCO2/kWh), and ~54% of their electricity came from fossil fuels.
AI.motivation: The rapid proliferation of hyperscale data centers (HDCs) in the US, driven by AI adoption, has raised concerns about this industry's environmental footprint, motivating a systematic assessment of their electricity consumption, sources, and attributable CO2 emissions.
AI.method: Compiled facility-level information on 403 US hyperscale data centers operating between May 2024 and April 2025, estimated electricity consumption, sources, and attributable CO2 emissions using the most recent EPA eGRID plant-level data, across different facility-load scenarios.
AI.result: HDCs consumed ~68–99 TWh electricity (~1.8% of total US consumption); ~54% of generation from fossil fuels; electricity-weighted average carbon intensity ~545 gCO2/kWh (48% above US grid average of 370 gCO2/kWh); attributable CO2 emissions ~37–54 Mt.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides an attributional tool for assessing the environmental footprint of hyperscale data centers using the most recent EPA eGRID plant-level data.

title: LadderMan: Learning Humanoid Perceptive Ladder Climbing
summary: Humanoid robots hold great promise for operating in human-centered environments, yet ladder climbing remains one of the most challenging tasks due to sparse footholds and handholds, complex whole-body coordination, and sensitivity to perception and control errors. We present \textbf{LadderMan}, a unified system that enables humanoid robots to robustly climb diverse ladders and perform manipulation under such constrained conditions. Our climbing policy is built on a scalable two-stage learning pipeline, where we use hybrid motion tracking to learn multiple climbing experts from a single reference motion, and distill these experts into a unified depth-based visuomotor climbing policy via hybrid imitation and reinforcement learning. To enable real-world deployment, we leverage vision foundation models to bridge the sim-to-real gap in depth perception. Building on the learned climbing policy, we further train a separate manipulation policy using a dual-agent formulation, allowing stable on-ladder manipulation via teleoperation. Experiments demonstrate that LadderMan achieves robust ladder climbing across a wide range of geometries, successfully transfers to real-world hardware in a zero-shot manner, and supports various manipulation tasks under challenging ladder constraints. Video results are available at https://ladderman-robot.github.io .

AI.tldr: LadderMan presents a unified system enabling humanoid robots to robustly climb diverse ladders and perform manipulation tasks under constrained ladder conditions, using a two-stage learning pipeline with hybrid imitation and reinforcement learning, vision foundation models for sim-to-real transfer, and a dual-agent formulation for manipulation.
AI.motivation: Ladder climbing for humanoid robots is extremely challenging due to sparse footholds/handholds, complex whole-body coordination, and sensitivity to perception/control errors, yet it is critical for operating in human-centered environments.
AI.method: A two-stage learning pipeline: (1) hybrid motion tracking to learn multiple climbing experts from a single reference motion, (2) distillation into a unified depth-based visuomotor climbing policy via hybrid imitation and reinforcement learning. Vision foundation models bridge sim-to-real depth perception gaps. A separate manipulation policy using a dual-agent formulation enables stable on-ladder teleoperation.
AI.result: LadderMan achieves robust ladder climbing across diverse geometries, zero-shot transfer to real-world hardware, and supports various manipulation tasks under challenging ladder constraints.
AI.conclusion: The proposed system successfully addresses the challenges of humanoid ladder climbing and manipulation, demonstrating both robustness and real-world deployability.

title: Minimizing the Hidden Cost of Scales: Graph-Guided Ultra-Low-Bit Quantization for Large Language Models
comment: Preprint. 18 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables, including appendix
summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is critical for the efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs). Recent ultra-low-bit PTQ methods rely on rigid weight-saliency assumptions or position heuristics, introducing substantial hidden scaling overhead. We propose SAGE-PTQ (Saliency-Aware Graph-guided Efficient PTQ), a novel ultra-low-bit quantization framework for LLMs that minimizes hidden scaling cost. SAGE-PTQ separates salient and unsalient weights using distributional statistics, then models subsampled unsalient weights as a sparse graph to estimate the optimal number of groups per layer. SAGE-PTQ applies dual-mode quantization, assigning multi-bit precision to salient weights and binarizing unsalient weights. To reduce scaling overhead, SAGE-PTQ uses one per-channel scale for salient weights and one scalar per unsalient group. Finally, SAGE-PTQ implements adaptive saliency thresholding to select the optimal saliency ratio per matrix. SAGE-PTQ achieves 1.03 weight bits and only 0.004 scaling bits per matrix on average, outperforming state-of-the-art methods such as BiLLM and PB-LLM. On LLaMA-3-8B, SAGE-PTQ achieves 6.74 WikiText2 perplexity, compared to 55.8 for BiLLM, while using less than 50% of BiLLM's GPU memory. On LLaMA-2-70B, SAGE-PTQ provides 1.5x faster decoding on one NVIDIA L40 GPU, demonstrating practical inference efficiency.

AI.tldr: SAGE-PTQ is a novel ultra-low-bit quantization framework for LLMs that separates salient and unsalient weights via distributional statistics, models unsalient weights as a sparse graph for optimal group allocation, and applies dual-mode quantization (multi-bit for salient, binary for unsalient) with minimal scaling overhead, achieving 1.03 weight bits and 0.004 scaling bits per matrix while outperforming BiLLM and PB-LLM in perplexity, memory, and inference speed.
AI.motivation: Existing ultra-low-bit PTQ methods rely on rigid weight-saliency assumptions or position heuristics, which introduce substantial hidden scaling overhead, motivating the need for a more efficient quantization framework that minimizes scaling cost while maintaining accuracy.
AI.method: The method separates salient and unsalient weights using distributional statistics, models subsampled unsalient weights as a sparse graph to estimate the optimal number of groups per layer, applies dual-mode quantization (multi-bit for salient, binarization for unsalient), uses one per-channel scale for salient weights and one scalar per unsalient group, and implements adaptive saliency thresholding to select the optimal saliency ratio per matrix.
AI.result: SAGE-PTQ achieves 1.03 weight bits and only 0.004 scaling bits per matrix on average. On LLaMA-3-8B, it achieves 6.74 WikiText2 perplexity vs. 55.8 for BiLLM, using less than 50% of BiLLM's GPU memory. On LLaMA-2-70B, it provides 1.5x faster decoding on one NVIDIA L40 GPU.
AI.conclusion: SAGE-PTQ demonstrates that modeling unsalient weights as a sparse graph with adaptive saliency thresholding can significantly reduce hidden scaling overhead in ultra-low-bit quantization, achieving superior perplexity, memory efficiency, and inference speed compared to state-of-the-art methods like BiLLM and PB-LLM.

title: TAGA: Terrain-aware Active Gaze Learning for Generalizable Agile Humanoid Locomotion
summary: Agile humanoid locomotion across diverse challenging terrain demands both wide perceptual coverage and precise local geometry understanding. Motivated by the way humans selectively look at relevant terrain during locomotion, we introduce TAGA, a Terrain-aware Active Gaze learning framework for Attention-based humanoid control. By fusing vision, proprioception, and motion commands, our framework guides the model to learn anticipatory cues and actively attend to specific areas of the height scan, selectively using these informative regions for the downstream network. This adaptively increases the information density of observations under tight onboard computational constraints, thus enabling fine-grained perceptive locomotion over larger-scale terrains. We find that such gaze behaviors can naturally emerge through reinforcement learning alone, without requiring additional supervision or explicit guidance, significantly improve training efficiency. As a result, the trained policy demonstrates robust and generalizable locomotion in simulation and on hardware, including reliable terrain-aware foothold selection, elevated-platform traversal, competitive sparse-foothold traversal, and the largest reported real-world gap traversal distance of 1.2m among perceptive humanoid locomotion systems, while maintaining stability under severe perceptual disturbances and environmental interference.

AI.tldr: TAGA is a terrain-aware active gaze framework that uses attention-based humanoid control, enabling robust locomotion across challenging terrains through emergent gaze behaviors learned via reinforcement learning, achieving record 1.2m gap traversal on real hardware.
AI.motivation: Agile humanoid locomotion across diverse challenging terrain requires both wide perceptual coverage and precise local geometry understanding, but onboard computational constraints limit information density. Humans selectively look at relevant terrain during locomotion, inspiring an active gaze approach.
AI.method: TAGA fuses vision, proprioception, and motion commands to guide the model to learn anticipatory cues and actively attend to specific areas of the height scan. Gaze behaviors emerge through reinforcement learning alone without additional supervision, adaptively increasing information density under computational constraints.
AI.result: The policy demonstrates robust and generalizable locomotion in simulation and on hardware, including terrain-aware foothold selection, elevated-platform traversal, competitive sparse-foothold traversal, and the largest reported real-world gap traversal distance of 1.2m among perceptive humanoid locomotion systems, while maintaining stability under severe perceptual disturbances.
AI.conclusion: Gaze behaviors can naturally emerge through reinforcement learning alone, significantly improving training efficiency and enabling fine-grained perceptive locomotion over larger-scale terrains without requiring additional supervision or explicit guidance.

title: Zero knowledge verification for frontier AI training is possible
summary: Frontier AI governance frameworks increasingly use cumulative training compute as the primary criterion for designating high-impact models, but enforcement rests on self-reporting because no technical verification primitive for training exists. Any future international agreement on frontier AI faces the same problem at higher stakes: coordinated regulation of technologies with significant externalities has historically rested on technical verification, without which agreements are declaratory. Recent governance analyses judge zero-knowledge proofs a promising candidate but currently impractical at frontier scale [26, 4]. We argue the impracticality is paradigm-bound rather than fundamental, and propose a verification architecture for frontier dense pre-training combining a pre-committed training specification, inter-node network observations, and on-the-fly Merkle commitments of intermediate computation, verified through a zero-knowledge Virtual Machine (zkVM) with native BF16/FP32 precompiles. The proof checks the actual floating-point computation the GPU performed rather than a fixed-point approximation, and preserves model-architecture confidentiality through a private training specification. The protocol produces three proof types: a genesis proof at initialisation, in-training step proofs across the run, and ex-ante attestations enforcing policy-relevant claims as running invariants, turning the training record into a governance-enforceable artefact. We estimate a deployable proof of concept within approximately 36 months at single-digit-percent training-side overhead, against a six-to-ten-year cycle for verification-grade custom silicon. Thirteen open research and engineering problems are catalogued as a research agenda for external contribution

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a zero-knowledge proof-based verification architecture for frontier AI training, using zkVM with native BF16/FP32 precompiles to prove correct floating-point computation on GPUs, enabling governance enforcement of training compute reporting with ~36-month deployable PoC at single-digit-percent overhead.
AI.motivation: Current frontier AI governance relies on self-reporting of cumulative training compute, which is unverifiable. No technical verification primitive exists for training, making any future international agreement declaratory rather than enforceable. Zero-knowledge proofs were deemed promising but impractical at frontier scale.
AI.method: The architecture combines: (1) pre-committed training specification, (2) inter-node network observations, (3) on-the-fly Merkle commitments of intermediate computation, verified through a zkVM with native BF16/FP32 precompiles. Produces genesis proofs, in-training step proofs, and ex-ante attestations. Preserves model-architecture confidentiality via private training specification.
AI.result: Proof of concept deployable within ~36 months at single-digit-percent training-side overhead, compared to 6-10 years for verification-grade custom silicon. Thirteen open problems catalogued as research agenda.
AI.conclusion: The impracticality of zero-knowledge proofs for frontier training verification is paradigm-bound rather than fundamental; the proposed architecture makes governance-enforceable training verification achievable in the near term.

title: A Novel Method with Encoder-Decoder for Cross-Sensor Adaptation in Surface Shape Sensing with Sparse Strain Sensors
summary: Performance variations in sensor arrays, caused by intrinsic differences or installation conditions, can lead to inconsistent results during shape sensing. To obtain accurate results, a large amount of data is usually required, and a separate model must be retrained for each sensor array, thereby increasing the cost and time of data acquisition, transmission, and computation. To address this issue, this work proposes an encoder-decoder architecture for surface shape sensing based on sparse strain sensors and further incorporates meta-learning and few-shot adaptation strategies to enable adaptation across different groups of sensor arrays. Experimental results demonstrate that, after the cross-sensor adaptation, a newly deployed sensor array achieves a sensing error of approximately 4.0 mm relying on less than 5.0% newly labeled data and requiring an adaptation time of under 1 second, which represents a substantial improvement from 23.0 mm error without adaptation and 20-minute data collection time required to train a new model. Moreover, the number of points with errors below 5.0 mm increased by more than 65.0%. These results indicate that the proposed method can substantially reduce the cost and training burden of surface shape sensing, and it has broad potential applications in soft robotics and wearable devices.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a meta-learning and few-shot adaptation-based encoder-decoder architecture for surface shape sensing using sparse strain sensors. It enables rapid adaptation across different sensor arrays with minimal data (less than 5%), reducing error from 23.0 mm to 4.0 mm and adaptation time to under 1 second, significantly lowering data acquisition and retraining costs.
AI.motivation: Performance variations in sensor arrays cause inconsistent shape sensing results. Traditional methods require large datasets and separate model retraining for each sensor array, which increases cost and time for data acquisition, transmission, and computation.
AI.method: An encoder-decoder architecture with meta-learning and few-shot adaptation strategies, enabling cross-sensor adaptation across different groups of sensor arrays using sparse strain sensors.
AI.result: After cross-sensor adaptation, a newly deployed sensor array achieves sensing error ~4.0 mm using less than 5.0% newly labeled data and adaptation time under 1 second, compared to 23.0 mm error without adaptation and 20-minute data collection for new model training. Points with errors below 5.0 mm increased by over 65%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method substantially reduces the cost and training burden of surface shape sensing, with broad potential applications in soft robotics and wearable devices.

title: Ten Headache Specialists versus Artificial Intelligence for Clinical Literature Summarization: A Critical Evaluation and Comparison
summary: Summarizing the latest medical literature to guide clinical decision-making is essential for evidence-based medicine and high-quality patient care. Yet clinicians face increasing challenges due to limited time with patients and a rapidly growing volume of published articles. Although retrieval-augmented large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in clinical summarization, human evaluations of their effectiveness in synthesizing broader scientific literature and direct comparisons to expert-written syntheses remain scarce. We constructed a RAG-based agentic AI framework using three state-of-the-art LLMs: Sonnet, GPT-4o, and Llama 3.1. A headache specialist created 13 questions, three for prompt optimization and ten for evaluation. Ten headache specialists across the United States and Canada each wrote a summary for one question, yielding four summaries per question (expert, Sonnet, GPT-4o, and Llama). The experts, blinded to authorship, critically evaluated the summaries, excluding the topic for which they wrote a summary, based on correctness, completeness, conciseness, and clinical utility, scoring each from 1 to 10 using standardized rubrics. They also ranked the summaries by preference and indicated whether they believed each summary was written by an expert or an LLM. Our study, comparing LLM- and expert-written literature summaries evaluated by headache specialists, showed that expert-written summaries were preferred, although experts sometimes found it challenging to distinguish between human- and AI-generated summaries. We also identified key expert-valued features beyond standard evaluation metrics that can guide future refinement of both human and AI literature summarization pipelines.

AI.tldr: A blinded evaluation by 10 headache specialists compared RAG-based LLM summaries (Sonnet, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1) with expert-written summaries on 10 clinical questions. Expert-written summaries were preferred, though experts sometimes struggled to distinguish AI from human summaries. Key features for improving summarization pipelines were identified.
AI.motivation: Clinicians face increasing challenges in keeping up with the rapidly growing volume of medical literature to guide evidence-based decision-making. Although retrieval-augmented LLMs show promise for clinical summarization, human evaluations of their effectiveness in synthesizing broader scientific literature and direct comparisons to expert-written syntheses remain scarce.
AI.method: Constructed a RAG-based agentic AI framework using Sonnet, GPT-4o, and Llama 3.1. A headache specialist created 13 questions (3 for prompt optimization, 10 for evaluation). Ten headache specialists each wrote one expert summary. Four summaries per question (expert, Sonnet, GPT-4o, Llama) were blinded and evaluated by the specialists on correctness, completeness, conciseness, and clinical utility (1-10 scale). Preference ranking and AI vs. human detection tasks were also conducted.
AI.result: Expert-written summaries were preferred over LLM-generated summaries overall. However, experts sometimes found it challenging to distinguish between human- and AI-generated summaries. Key expert-valued features beyond standard metrics were identified to guide future refinement of summarization pipelines.
AI.conclusion: While expert-written summaries remain preferred, LLM-generated summaries can be difficult to distinguish from human ones. The identified expert-valued features can inform improvements to both human and AI literature summarization approaches.

title: Learning of Robot Safety Policies via Adversarial Synthetic Scenarios
summary: In this work, we propose an agentic gamification framework for hazard-informed learning of robot safety policies through synthetic scenarios. We model scenario generation as an adversarial game between two agents: a Red Team that explores the space of potential failures by constructing hazardous situations, and a Blue Team that incrementally refines safety policies to prevent them. This iterative process enables efficient discovery of high-risk edge cases that are unlikely to be captured through random simulation or manual enumeration. By combining classical risk modeling with adversarial scenario generation and modern learning paradigms, this work provides a scalable pathway for embedding safety into Physical AI systems operating in complex real-world environments. The paper describes ongoing work. The contribution is a problem formulation and a proposed solution architecture.

AI.tldr: Proposes an agentic gamification framework where Red and Blue teams adversarially generate hazardous scenarios and refine safety policies for robot learning, enabling discovery of high-risk edge cases.
AI.motivation: High-risk edge cases in robot safety are unlikely to be captured through random simulation or manual enumeration, necessitating a more systematic and scalable approach to hazard discovery and policy refinement.
AI.method: Models scenario generation as an adversarial game between a Red Team (exploring failure spaces by constructing hazardous situations) and a Blue Team (incrementally refining safety policies), combining classical risk modeling with adversarial generation and modern learning paradigms.
AI.result: The paper describes ongoing work; the result is a problem formulation and a proposed solution architecture rather than empirical results.
AI.conclusion: This framework provides a scalable pathway for embedding safety into Physical AI systems operating in complex real-world environments through adversarial hazard discovery and iterative policy refinement.

title: Brick-Composer: Using MLLMs for Assembly with Diverse Bricks
summary: We dream of AI agents that can read arbitrary designs and construct real-world objects from reusable building blocks. As a first step toward this vision, we study whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) possess the visual grounding and spatial reasoning capabilities required for brick assembly. We formulate brick assembly as a sequential decision-making problem, where each step involves two subtasks: brick selection, identifying the target brick from candidate components, and brick pose estimation, predicting where and how the selected brick should be placed. To support this study, we introduce BC-Bench (Brick Construction Benchmark), the first benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on assembly with diverse bricks. Experiments show that current state-of-the-art MLLMs remain far from reliable builders, struggling with fine-grained brick selection and failing at precise pose estimation. To bridge this gap, we propose Brick-Composer, a learning framework that equips MLLMs with assembly skills through three complementary signals: Human Design Sparks, which provide affordance-rich construction demonstrations; World Feedback, which grounds predicted actions in visual and physical consequences; and Synthetic Experience, which scales learning beyond existing object designs. Brick-Composer improves brick selection accuracy by over three times, substantially reduces pose estimation errors, and raises strict step-level assembly success from less than 1% to around 15%. After training, a Qwen-3-8B can correctly compose up to 42% of the steps for a complete object, suggesting that MLLMs can acquire assembly capabilities through targeted, physically grounded learning.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces BC-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on brick assembly, where current models perform poorly. The authors propose Brick-Composer, a learning framework using Human Design Sparks, World Feedback, and Synthetic Experience, which improves brick selection accuracy 3x, reduces pose estimation errors, and raises step-level assembly success from <1% to ~15%, with a Qwen-3-8B achieving 42% step-level correctness.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to explore whether MLLMs possess the visual grounding and spatial reasoning needed for brick assembly, and to enable AI agents that can read designs and construct real-world objects from reusable building blocks.
AI.method: The authors formulate brick assembly as sequential decision-making with two subtasks: brick selection and brick pose estimation. They build BC-Bench for evaluation and propose Brick-Composer, which trains MLLMs using three signals: Human Design Sparks (affordance-rich demonstrations), World Feedback (visual/physical consequences of actions), and Synthetic Experience (scaling beyond existing designs).
AI.result: Current MLLMs perform poorly on BC-Bench. Brick-Composer improves brick selection accuracy by over 3x, reduces pose estimation errors substantially, and raises strict step-level assembly success from <1% to ~15%. A Qwen-3-8B using this framework can correctly compose up to 42% of steps for a complete object.
AI.conclusion: MLLMs can acquire assembly capabilities through targeted, physically grounded learning, though they remain far from reliable builders in the brick assembly domain.

title: Towards a Data Flywheel for Embodied Intelligence in Logistics
summary: Embodied intelligence is moving from laboratory demonstrations toward industrial deployment, with the logistics industry serving as a key application scenario. Learning-based policies offer a promising path beyond traditional perception-planning-control pipelines, but their scalability depends on how embodied data can be collected, organized, and reused. This research studies a data-centric framework for industrial embodied intelligence by constructing a logistics data flywheel. Our framework converts daily operations into reusable data assets, uses World Models to generate reliable supervision for long-tail parcel manipulation, and feeds deployment feedback back into policy improvement. As an initial result, \textit{WM-DAgger} introduces a World-Model-based data aggregation framework that synthesizes out-of-distribution recovery data for robust imitation learning. Building on this result, ongoing work explores how large-scale in-the-wild multimodal data, including labeled human demonstrations, unlabeled operational videos, and system-level robot logs, can be aligned for policy learning and transformed into feedback for continual system improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a data-centric framework for industrial embodied intelligence using a logistics data flywheel, where daily operations are converted into reusable data assets, World Models generate supervision for long-tail tasks, and deployment feedback improves policies. Initial results introduce WM-DAgger, a World-Model-based data aggregation method for robust imitation learning, with ongoing work exploring alignment of large-scale multimodal data for continual policy improvement.
AI.motivation: To enable scalable deployment of embodied intelligence in logistics by moving beyond traditional perception-planning-control pipelines, addressing the challenge of how embodied data can be collected, organized, and reused for learning-based policies.
AI.method: A data-centric framework structured as a logistics data flywheel: (1) converting daily operations into reusable data assets, (2) using World Models to generate reliable supervision for long-tail parcel manipulation, (3) feeding deployment feedback back into policy improvement. Specifically, WM-DAgger synthesizes out-of-distribution recovery data for robust imitation learning.
AI.result: WM-DAgger introduces a World-Model-based data aggregation framework that synthesizes out-of-distribution recovery data for robust imitation learning. Ongoing work investigates aligning large-scale in-the-wild multimodal data (labeled human demonstrations, unlabeled operational videos, system-level robot logs) for policy learning.
AI.conclusion: The data flywheel framework shows promise for scaling industrial embodied intelligence. Future work involves transforming multimodal operational data into feedback for continual system improvement, closing the loop from deployment back to policy refinement.

title: Insurance of Agentic AI
summary: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are transforming the risk landscape by extending beyond information generation to autonomous planning, tool invocation, decision execution, and persistent modification of digital and physical environments. These capabilities introduce novel exposures that do not fit neatly within traditional insurance categories such as cyber, professional liability, product liability, or directors and officers coverage. This paper examines the emerging insurance market for agentic AI and develops a framework for understanding its underwriting, pricing, reinsurance, and product-design implications. We characterize agentic AI as a continuum of autonomy and delegated authority, emphasizing the distinction between informational outputs and systems capable of independently generating insured events through external actions. We analyze major risk pathways, including hallucinations, prompt-injection attacks, autonomous decision errors, model drift, dependency failures, and cyber-physical harms, and evaluate how existing insurance products are adapting to address these exposures. The paper further proposes an actuarial framework based on exposure assessment, scenario analysis, dependency mapping, and accumulation-risk management, drawing parallels to the evolution of cyber insurance. Finally, we present a coordinated insurance architecture that integrates cyber, technology errors and omissions, product liability, performance-warranty, and affirmative AI-liability coverages through explicit allocation mechanisms and dedicated AI aggregates. The analysis suggests that the future of agentic-AI insurance lies not in a single monoline product but in a layered ecosystem of complementary coverages supported by improved governance, transparency, telemetry, and regulatory clarity.

AI.tldr: This paper examines the emerging insurance market for agentic AI systems—AI that can autonomously plan, act, and modify environments—and proposes a framework for underwriting, pricing, reinsurance, and product design. It argues that agentic AI introduces novel risks beyond traditional insurance categories and advocates for a layered ecosystem of complementary coverages rather than a single monoline product.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems extend beyond information generation to autonomous actions, creating novel risk exposures that existing insurance products (cyber, professional liability, product liability, D&O) are ill-equipped to handle. A structured insurance framework is needed to address these emerging risks.
AI.method: The paper characterizes agentic AI along a continuum of autonomy and delegated authority, analyzes major risk pathways (hallucinations, prompt-injection, decision errors, model drift, dependency failures, cyber-physical harms), evaluates how current insurance products are adapting, and proposes an actuarial framework using exposure assessment, scenario analysis, dependency mapping, and accumulation-risk management.
AI.result: The paper proposes a coordinated insurance architecture integrating cyber, tech E&O, product liability, performance warranty, and affirmative AI-liability coverages with explicit allocation mechanisms and dedicated AI aggregates. It finds that the future of agentic-AI insurance is a layered ecosystem of complementary coverages rather than a monoline product.
AI.conclusion: Effective insurance for agentic AI requires improved governance, transparency, telemetry, and regulatory clarity to support a layered ecosystem of coordinated coverages.

title: World-Language-Action Model for Unified World Modeling, Language Reasoning, and Action Synthesis
summary: We propose world-language-action (WLA) models as a new class of embodied foundation models. WLA takes textual instructions, images, and robot states as inputs to jointly predict textual subtasks, subgoal images, and robot actions, conjoining the \emph{world modeling interface} to learn from extensive egocentric videos as in the world-action model (WAM) and the \emph{language reasoning} capacities to solve complex long-horizon tasks as in vision-language-action (VLA) models. At the core of WLA lies an \emph{autoregressive (AR)} Transformer backbone, instead of a bidirectional diffusion Transformer as in WAMs, to predict the \emph{next state}, comprising the \emph{semantic-level} textual intention and complementary \emph{fine-grained} physical dynamics. The physical dynamics are supervised by the world modeling objective based on a dedicated World Expert, and are leveraged to ease the characterization of the state-action correlation for the Action Expert. WLA leverages meta-queries to make the world prediction \emph{implicitly} impact the action generation so that the former can be disabled during inference. The world prediction can also be activated to enable test-time scaling for improved robot control. Our WLA-0 prototype, with 2B active parameters, achieves 40 ms per inference on an NVIDIA RTX 5090. Evaluations across simulated and real-world environments demonstrate that WLA-0 achieves state-of-the-art multi-task and long-horizon learning abilities, e.g., 92.94\% success rate on RoboTwin2.0 Clean and 56.5\% success rate on RMBench. WLA-0 also holds the promise to learn novel tasks directly from \emph{cross-embodiment robot videos} without action annotations.

AI.tldr: WLA models unify world modeling (WAM) and vision-language-action (VLA) into an autoregressive Transformer that jointly predicts textual subtasks, subgoal images, and robot actions. The 2B-parameter WLA-0 achieves 92.94% success on RoboTwin2.0 Clean and can learn from cross-embodiment videos without action annotations.
AI.motivation: Existing embodied foundation models either lack language reasoning for long-horizon tasks (WAMs) or cannot leverage large-scale egocentric video data (VLAs). WLA aims to bridge this gap by jointly modeling world dynamics and language-guided action generation.
AI.method: WLA uses an autoregressive Transformer backbone to predict the next state (textual intention + fine-grained physical dynamics). Physical dynamics are supervised by a World Expert objective, and meta-queries enable implicit world-modeling influence on action generation, which can be disabled at inference or activated for test-time scaling.
AI.result: WLA-0 (2B active parameters, 40 ms/inference on RTX 5090) achieves 92.94% success on RoboTwin2.0 Clean and 56.5% on RMBench, outperforming prior methods. It also learns novel tasks from cross-embodiment videos without action labels.
AI.conclusion: WLA models offer a unified framework combining world modeling and language reasoning, achieving SOTA multi-task and long-horizon performance while supporting test-time scaling and cross-embodiment video learning.

title: Output Type Before Quality: A Standards-Derived XAI Admissibility Rubric for Autonomous-Driving Safety
summary:
Safety standards for ML-based autonomous driving specify the kind of evidence an assurance case must contain (directed cause-and-effect chains, quantified interventional effects, named root-cause variables), yet the XAI literature is organised by output type and technique family (saliency maps, feature attribution, counterfactuals, causal graphs, language traces). SHAP, the most-recommended ADS XAI method, returns a ranked feature list that no implementation effort can convert into a directed chain (Fig.1). We name this mismatch the evidence-type gap.
  From AMLAS, ISO 26262, ISO21448, ISO/PAS 8800 we derive 19 testable evidentiary criteria across 7 lifecycle stages with representative clause-cited derivations and score six XAI method classes structurally.
  Causal XAI emerges as structurally required to satisfy the derived criteria at three stages: hazard identification (+62% rubric gap), incident investigation (+50%), and data management (+50%); the verdict set is stable across thresholds T in (0%, 50%]$ and survives a worst-case single-cell flip down to T = 25%. At the remaining four stages, correlational or language-based methods are comparable or sufficient. The rubric identifies structural admissibility (necessary but not sufficient for compliance): an admissible method's specific output content may still be wrong, and validating that fidelity (the edges a fitted SCM produces, the cause a trace names) is the open assurance challenge. A single-VLA proof of concept on 1,996 real-world driving clips (79,840 rows, ten splits) is consistent with each method's observed output type matching its rubric prediction. XAI method selection for ADS safety assurance should be driven by lifecycle-stage evidence demand, not by method popularity.

AI.tldr: There is a mismatch (evidence-type gap) between what ADS safety standards require (directed cause-and-effect chains, quantified interventional effects) and what popular XAI methods like SHAP provide (ranked feature lists). The authors derive 19 evidentiary criteria from safety standards, score six XAI method classes, and find Causal XAI is structurally necessary for three lifecycle stages, while other methods suffice for four stages.
AI.motivation: To identify and formalize the "evidence-type gap" between safety assurance standards for ML-based autonomous driving systems (ADS) and the output types produced by current XAI methods, and to provide structured guidance for method selection based on lifecycle-stage evidence demand rather than popularity.
AI.method: Derived 19 testable evidentiary criteria from AMLAS, ISO 26262, ISO 21448, and ISO/PAS 8800 across 7 lifecycle stages; scored six XAI method classes (saliency maps, feature attribution, counterfactuals, causal graphs, language traces, and others) structurally; validated with a single-VLA proof of concept on 1,996 real-world driving clips (79,840 rows, ten splits).
AI.result: Causal XAI is structurally required for hazard identification (+62% rubric gap), incident investigation (+50%), and data management (+50%); verdicts stable across thresholds T in (0%, 50%] and survive worst-case single-cell flip to T=25%. For the remaining four stages, correlational or language-based methods are sufficient. Proof-of-concept matched rubric predictions.
AI.conclusion: XAI method selection for ADS safety assurance should be driven by lifecycle-stage evidence demand, not method popularity. Structural admissibility is necessary but not sufficient—fidelity validation remains an open challenge.

title: Merging model-based control with multi-agent reinforcement learning for multi-agent cooperative teaming strategies
summary: In this work, we propose a framework that combines multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) with model-based control to achieve safe, dynamically feasible actions in cooperative multi-agent tasks. Multi-agent reinforcement learning provides the advantage of learning cooperative policies for multi-agent teams from discrete non-differentiable rewards in a long planning horizon. Model-predictive control is robust and offers safe, dynamically feasible actions in a fast replanning framework for short horizons. We propose an algorithm that extends actor-critic model predictive control for MARL which we refer to as multi-agent actor-critic model predictive control (MA-AC-MPC). We demonstrate the capabilities of this algorithm by applying it to a multi-agent pursuit-evasion scenario. Specifically, we compare the evader team's strategy using the MA-AC-MPC model and a multi-layer perceptron model (MA-AC-MLP). The pursuer team uses augmented proportional navigation as it is accepted as an advanced adversarial control law. We also provide an example with a heterogeneous environment where a drone and omni-wheeled rover cooperate to achieve repeatable and successful landing with 100% success rate in hardware for MA-AC-MPC compared to 60% for MA-AC-MLP. We demonstrate the robustness of the proposed MA-AC-MPC algorithm in hardware for both environments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MA-AC-MPC, a framework combining multi-agent reinforcement learning with model predictive control for safe, dynamically feasible cooperative multi-agent tasks, demonstrating superior performance over MA-AC-MLP in pursuit-evasion scenarios and heterogeneous drone-rover landing tasks with 100% hardware success rate.
AI.motivation: To combine the long-horizon cooperative policy learning strengths of MARL with the short-horizon safety, robustness, and dynamic feasibility of model predictive control for multi-agent systems.
AI.method: Extends actor-critic model predictive control to the multi-agent setting (MA-AC-MPC), integrating MARL with MPC to leverage both long-horizon reward learning and short-horizon safe replanning.
AI.result: MA-AC-MPC achieved 100% success rate in hardware for heterogeneous drone-rover landing vs. 60% for MA-AC-MLP; also validated in multi-agent pursuit-evasion scenarios.
AI.conclusion: MA-AC-MPC demonstrates superior safety, robustness, and success rates over purely learned methods (MA-AC-MLP) in both simulated and real-world cooperative multi-agent tasks.

title: PSEBench: A Controllable and Verifiable Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs in Patient Safety Event Triage
summary: Patient safety event triage, determining whether a clinical event is reportable under jurisdiction-specific policy, is a high-stakes task typically performed manually by patient safety experts. Although LLMs may support this workflow, reliable evaluation is limited by the lack of benchmarks to capture evidence-grounded policy reasoning, proactive information seeking for incomplete reports, and principled abstention in irreducibly ambiguous cases. We address this gap with a policy-grounded construction methodology centered on the clause card, a structured representation that factorizes regulatory text into auditable decision specifications. Combining clause cards with anchor-driven instantiation and closed-loop verification, our scalable pipeline produces narratives with by-construction ground truth and naturally supports generating missing information and uncertain variants. We instantiate this method on Minnesota's 29 Reportable Adverse Health Events, producing PSEBench, a 5,074-case benchmark with an agentic evaluation environment. Evaluation on 15 representative LLMs reveals consistent capability trends, demonstrates the benchmark's utility, and identifies actionable gaps toward reliable LLM-based patient safety event triage.

AI.tldr: PSEBench is a new 5,074-case benchmark for evaluating LLMs on patient safety event triage, built using clause cards to ground regulatory reasoning, support proactive information seeking, and handle ambiguous cases. Evaluation of 15 LLMs reveals capability trends and actionable gaps.
AI.motivation: Patient safety event triage is a high-stakes task done manually, but LLM adoption is limited by the lack of benchmarks that capture evidence-grounded policy reasoning, proactive information seeking, and principled abstention in ambiguous cases.
AI.method: The authors propose a policy-grounded construction methodology using clause cards (structured representations of regulatory text), combined with anchor-driven instantiation and closed-loop verification to produce narratives with ground truth, missing information, and uncertain variants. This is instantiated on Minnesota's 29 Reportable Adverse Health Events to create PSEBench.
AI.result: PSEBench contains 5,074 cases with an agentic evaluation environment. Evaluation of 15 representative LLMs shows consistent capability trends, demonstrates benchmark utility, and identifies actionable gaps for reliable LLM-based triage.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark effectively captures gaps in LLM reasoning for patient safety event triage, highlighting where models fall short in policy-grounded reasoning and proactive information seeking.

title: RealDexUMI: A Wearable Universal Manipulation Interface for Dexterous Robot Learning
summary: Learning dexterous manipulation requires demonstrations that preserve fine hand-object interactions while remaining executable at deployment. Existing pipelines either lose deployable dexterity through retargeting or embodiment conversion, or rely on robot-specific teleoperation that is costly to scale and often lacks intuitive, contact-aware control for dexterous data collection. We present RealDexUMI, a wearable universal manipulation interface built around a shared dexterous end-effector module that integrates a lightweight dexterous hand, in-hand vision, and fingertip tactile sensing. A palm-side isomorphic teleoperation glove maps human finger inputs to robot-hand joint commands, enabling real-time, retargeting-free, intuitive, and precise hand control. The shared hand and sensing modules yield zero-gap end-effector data, with matched in-hand observations, tactile signals, contacts, and hand actions between collection and deployment. Across eight real-robot tasks spanning fine-grained, contact-rich, long-horizon, and bimanual manipulation, policies trained on RealDexUMI data achieve an average success rate of 88.75%, generalize to unseen initial poses, and transfer across three embodiments. Website: https://research.beingbeyond.com/realdexumi

AI.tldr: RealDexUMI is a wearable universal manipulation interface with a shared dexterous end-effector module combining a lightweight hand, in-hand vision, and fingertip tactile sensing. Using a palm-side isomorphic teleoperation glove for retargeting-free control, it achieves zero-gap between data collection and deployment. Policies trained on its data achieve 88.75% average success across eight tasks, generalize to unseen poses, and transfer across three embodiments.
AI.motivation: Existing dexterous manipulation pipelines either lose deployable dexterity through retargeting/embodiment conversion, or rely on robot-specific teleoperation that is costly to scale and lacks intuitive, contact-aware control for data collection.
AI.method: RealDexUMI uses a shared dexterous end-effector module (lightweight hand, in-hand vision, fingertip tactile sensing) with a palm-side isomorphic teleoperation glove that maps human finger inputs directly to robot-hand joint commands, eliminating retargeting and ensuring matched observations between collection and deployment.
AI.result: Across eight real-robot tasks (fine-grained, contact-rich, long-horizon, bimanual), policies achieve 88.75% average success rate, generalize to unseen initial poses, and transfer across three embodiments.
AI.conclusion: RealDexUMI provides an intuitive, retargeting-free, and scalable solution for collecting dexterous manipulation demonstrations that preserve fine hand-object interactions and transfer seamlessly to deployment across different robot embodiments.

title: Step-by-Step Optimization-like Reasoning in LLMs over Expanding Search Spaces
summary: Verifiable reward training has improved mathematical and coding reasoning, but these domains capture only part of step-by-step decision making. Many real-world tasks require finding a high-value feasible plan among many valid alternatives. We introduce OPT*, a scalable family of optimization-style tasks for training and evaluating LLM step-by-step optimization-like reasoning along a complexity axis: each task provides a feasibility checker and evaluator, while a complexity parameter expands the search space without requiring new human labels. This motivates studying these tasks in two regimes: (i) solver-guided online policy optimization, which uses a solver as a value oracle for partial states and applies rank-based reward shaping to reinforce better next steps, and (ii) search-based offline RL when such solvers are unavailable. Theoretically, we relate success in large search spaces to the information a reasoner extracts per unit of search budget. Empirically, we ablate the ingredients that make search efficient on OPT* and show that training on OPT* improves step-by-step optimization-like reasoning.

AI.tldr: OPT* introduces scalable optimization-style tasks for LLMs that require finding high-value feasible plans using step-by-step reasoning, with complexity-controllable search spaces. It proposes two training regimes (solver-guided online RL and search-based offline RL) and shows that training on OPT* improves optimization-like reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing verifiable reward training focuses on math and coding, which capture only part of step-by-step decision making. Many real-world tasks require finding a high-value feasible plan among many valid alternatives, a capability not well-addressed by current benchmarks.
AI.method: OPT* provides a family of optimization tasks with a feasibility checker and evaluator, and a complexity parameter to expand search space without new labels. Two training regimes are studied: (i) solver-guided online policy optimization with rank-based reward shaping, and (ii) search-based offline RL when solvers are unavailable. The paper also theoretically relates success in large search spaces to information extracted per unit of search budget.
AI.result: Empirical ablations show which ingredients make search efficient on OPT*, and training on OPT* improves step-by-step optimization-like reasoning.
AI.conclusion: OPT* effectively bridges the gap between existing verifiable reward training and real-world optimization tasks, providing a scalable framework to improve LLM optimization-like reasoning.

title: Gotta Grow Fast: Design and Benchmarking of a Tip Mount for High-Speed Vine Robots
comment: Accepted to IEEE Robotics & Automation Letters
summary: Soft, growing vine robots extend through tip eversion, a mechanism that enables navigation through cluttered environments. However, integrating cameras and other sensors at the tip is uniquely challenging because the material forming the tip is constantly renewed as the robot grows. This continual material turnover, combined with friction between internal layers, added tip weight, and fabric constriction, complicates sensor and tool mounting. These limitations hinder the deployment of vine robots for inspection and search tasks, where rapid growth while carrying tip-mounted sensors is essential. In this work, we present a triangular roller tip mount that reduces internal resistance during growth by rolling rather than sliding against the robot body. The design was refined through iterative failure analysis, enabling, for the first time, consistent eversion on a TPU-coated ripstop nylon vine robot. To quantitatively evaluate mount performance, we introduce a custom testbed that isolates tip mounting effects by measuring tail tension during eversion. Comparative experiments across multiple mount variants, including prior designs, show that our triangular roller mount achieves the lowest tail tension and most repeatable growth performance. These results establish both a validated tip mount design and a repeatable benchmarking framework for advancing sensor and tool integration in soft growing robots. CAD for the mount and testbed is available at: https://sprout-mitll.github.io/tip_mounts/.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a triangular roller tip mount for vine robots that reduces internal resistance during growth by rolling instead of sliding, enabling consistent eversion on TPU-coated ripstop nylon. A custom testbed measures tail tension to evaluate performance, showing the roller mount achieves the lowest tension and most repeatable growth compared to prior designs.
AI.motivation: Integrating cameras and sensors at the tip of vine robots is challenging because the tip material is constantly renewed during growth. Friction, added tip weight, and fabric constriction complicate sensor mounting, hindering deployment for inspection and search tasks.
AI.method: A triangular roller tip mount that reduces internal resistance by rolling rather than sliding. Iterative failure analysis refined the design. A custom testbed isolates tip mounting effects by measuring tail tension during eversion for quantitative evaluation.
AI.result: The triangular roller mount achieves the lowest tail tension and most repeatable growth performance across multiple mount variants, including prior designs. It enables, for the first time, consistent eversion on a TPU-coated ripstop nylon vine robot.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes both a validated tip mount design and a repeatable benchmarking framework for advancing sensor and tool integration in soft growing robots.

title: Severity-Aware Curriculum Learning with Multi-Model Response Selection for Medical Text Generation
summary: Telehealth systems have become increasingly important for delivering accessible and timely medical information. Existing large language models often struggle to provide consistent and contextually appropriate medical responses across varying levels of case severity. This limitation highlights the need for models that can effectively adapt to the progressive complexity in medical queries. To address this challenge, we introduce a severity-aware multi-model framework that integrates curriculum training strategy with relevance-based response selection. The proposed framework employs a three-stage curriculum learning strategy, where each model is trained sequentially on mild, moderate, and critical cases to progressively acquire domain knowledge. The approach utilizes five large language models, each independently trained under the same curriculum scheme. During inference, all models generate candidate responses, and the most appropriate response is selected as the final output. The framework is trained and evaluated on the MAQA dataset, which provides annotated medical question-answer pairs. Experimental results evaluated using BERTScore demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to both baseline and fine-tuned models, attaining 86.71% in the baseline setting and 90.30% after fine-tuning. These results highlight the effectiveness of combining curriculum learning with multi-model response selection in improving response quality and relevance in medical text generation.

AI.tldr: A severity-aware multi-model framework combining curriculum learning (mild→moderate→critical) with multi-model response selection achieves superior medical text generation performance (86.71% baseline, 90.30% fine-tuned BERTScore) on the MAQA dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing LLMs struggle to provide consistent and contextually appropriate medical responses across varying levels of case severity, necessitating models that can adapt to progressive complexity in medical queries.
AI.method: A three-stage curriculum learning strategy trains five LLMs sequentially on mild, moderate, and critical cases. During inference, all models generate candidate responses, and the most appropriate response is selected via relevance-based response selection.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves 86.71% BERTScore in the baseline setting and 90.30% after fine-tuning, outperforming both baseline and fine-tuned models on the MAQA dataset.
AI.conclusion: Combining curriculum learning with multi-model response selection effectively improves response quality and relevance in medical text generation.

title: Sample-efficient Low-level Motion Planning for Robotic Manipulation Tasks via Zero-shot Transfer Learning
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, International Conference on Artificial Neural Networks (ICANN) 2026 conference accepted
summary: As robotic systems become more sophisticated, the growing complexity of their motion planning models and the longer training times pose substantial challenges. Evolutionary algorithms such as the Sample-efficient Cross-Entropy Method (iCEM) have recently demonstrated promising potential for low-level real-time planning by leveraging efficient knowledge reuse strategies to improve performance. Although effective in many control tasks, iCEM's performance can be constrained in more complex scenarios, particularly those requiring stacking, sliding, and shelf placement.
