AI.motivation: Existing RAG cache fusion selectors face a dilemma between quality and efficiency: fast query-agnostic or final-layer selectors may miss relevant evidence, while full-view query-aware selectors stall the layer-wise cache-fusion pipeline by requiring broad context and layer visibility before recomputation.
AI.method: QCFuse is a compressed-view query-aware selector for RAG cache fusion. It uses chunk-anchor query probing to condition user-query states on compact per-chunk anchors and critical-layer profiling to identify recomputation tokens without requiring full-layer inspection. The system is implemented in SGLang.
AI.result: QCFuse reaches full-prefill-level quality. At matched quality, it achieves an average prefill-time speedup of 1.7x over full prefill and 1.5x over ProphetKV (the strongest quality-preserving baseline).
AI.conclusion: QCFuse achieves full-prefill-level quality while delivering significant prefill-time speedups: 1.7x over full prefill and 1.5x over ProphetKV on average across four open-weight LLMs and six datasets.

title: Retry Policy Gradients in Continuous Action Spaces
summary: Retry-based objectives such as pass@K and max@K optimize the best return obtained from multiple sampled trajectories, and recent work has shown that they can promote exploration without explicit exploration bonuses. In discrete action spaces, ReMax was shown to do so by adapting to return uncertainty. In this work, we introduce pathwise derivative estimators for retry objectives and use them to extend ReMax to continuous action spaces. We study the resulting learning dynamics and show that, even with deterministic rewards, ReMax can encourage stochastic exploration by reshaping the policy-gradient landscape. In particular, it alters gradients both in direction, biasing updates toward higher policy entropy, and in magnitude, damping gradients and slowing convergence. We further show that Adam's adaptive normalization can mitigate this damping, depending on its numerical stabilization parameter. Empirically, we instantiate this objective as ReMax Actor-Critic (ReMAC), an off-policy actor--critic algorithm that optimizes the ReMax objective using a pathwise derivative estimator. Our experiments show that ReMAC can promote higher policy entropy without entropy regularization and achieves performance comparable to SAC.

AI.tldr: The paper extends ReMax retry-based objectives to continuous action spaces using pathwise derivative estimators, showing it promotes stochastic exploration and entropy through gradient reshaping. The proposed ReMAC algorithm achieves performance comparable to SAC without entropy regularization.
AI.motivation: Retry-based objectives (pass@K, max@K) have shown promise for promoting exploration in discrete action spaces (via ReMax), but their application to continuous action spaces remains unexplored.
AI.method: Introduces pathwise derivative estimators for retry objectives, extending ReMax to continuous action spaces. Proposes ReMAC (ReMax Actor-Critic), an off-policy actor-critic algorithm using this estimator. Analyzes how ReMax reshapes policy gradients in direction (toward higher entropy) and magnitude (damping convergence), and how Adam's normalization mitigates damping.
AI.result: ReMAC promotes higher policy entropy without entropy regularization and achieves performance comparable to SAC on continuous control tasks.
AI.conclusion: Retry-based objectives can be effectively extended to continuous action spaces, where they naturally encourage exploration and entropy through gradient reshaping effects.

title: Retrospective Harness Optimization: Improving LLM Agents via Self-Preference over Trajectory Rollouts
summary: AI agents rely on a harness of skills, tools, and workflows to solve complex problems. Continually improving this harness is essential for adapting to new tasks. However, existing optimization methods typically require ground-truth validation sets, yet such labeled data is difficult to acquire in practical deployment settings. To address this problem, we introduce Retrospective Harness Optimization (RHO), a self-supervised method that optimizes the agent harness using only past trajectories. Specifically, RHO selects a diverse coreset of challenging tasks from past trajectories and re-solves them in parallel. The agent analyzes these rollouts using self-validation and self-consistency, then generates candidate harness updates and selects the most effective one by its own pairwise self-preference. We evaluate RHO across three diverse domains, spanning software engineering, technical work, and knowledge work. Notably, a single optimization round improves the pass rate on SWE-Bench Pro from 59% to 78% without any external grading. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that RHO effectively targets prior failure modes. As a result, the optimized harness alters the agent's behavior patterns and sustains higher accuracy during long-horizon sessions.

AI.tldr: RHO is a self-supervised method that optimizes AI agent harnesses using only past trajectories, without requiring ground-truth validation sets. It selects challenging tasks, re-solves them, analyzes rollouts via self-validation/self-consistency, and generates harness updates via self-preference. It improved SWE-Bench Pro pass rate from 59% to 78% in one round.
AI.motivation: Existing agent harness optimization methods require ground-truth validation sets, which are difficult to acquire in practical deployment settings. This creates a bottleneck for continually improving agent capabilities to adapt to new tasks.
AI.method: RHO operates in four steps: (1) select a diverse coreset of challenging tasks from past trajectories; (2) re-solve them in parallel; (3) analyze rollouts using self-validation and self-consistency; (4) generate candidate harness updates and select the best via pairwise self-preference.
AI.result: RHO improves SWE-Bench Pro pass rate from 59% to 78% in a single optimization round without external grading. It effectively targets prior failure modes, alters agent behavior patterns, and sustains higher accuracy during long-horizon sessions across three domains (software engineering, technical work, knowledge work).
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised harness optimization (RHO) is a practical and effective approach for improving AI agents without labeled data, demonstrating significant gains across diverse domains and sustained improvements in long-horizon tasks.

title: Towards World Models in Biomedical Research
summary: A central goal of biomedicine is to understand, predict and ultimately control the dynamic mechanisms by which biological systems respond to perturbations, disease progression and therapeutic intervention. Although foundation models and large language models have accelerated biomedical data interpretation, most current systems remain focused on static pattern recognition rather than prospective simulation of biological futures. Here we propose biomedical world models as a paradigm for AI-driven discovery. These models learn latent representations of molecular, cellular, tissue and clinical states, together with intervention-conditioned dynamics that allow future trajectories to be simulated before actions are taken. We discuss how biomedical world models could function as data engines, environment simulators and scientific planning substrates across applications including virtual cells, organoids, virtual patients and surgical simulation. We outline the data infrastructure, evaluation benchmarks, safety constraints and governance frameworks required. Biomedical world models may provide a foundation for simulation-guided, closed-loop and experimentally actionable biomedical discovery.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes biomedical world models as a new AI paradigm for simulating biological system dynamics over time, moving beyond static pattern recognition to enable prospective simulation of molecular, cellular, tissue, and clinical state trajectories under interventions.
AI.motivation: Current AI systems excel at static pattern recognition but cannot prospectively simulate how biological systems evolve over time in response to perturbations, disease progression, or treatments. This limits their utility for predictive and interventional biomedicine.
AI.method: The authors propose biomedical world models that learn latent representations of multi-scale biological states (molecular, cellular, tissue, clinical) paired with intervention-conditioned dynamics models to simulate future trajectories before real-world actions are taken.
AI.result: The framework is discussed conceptually for applications including virtual cells, organoids, virtual patients, and surgical simulation. The paper also identifies required data infrastructure, evaluation benchmarks, safety constraints, and governance frameworks.
AI.conclusion: Biomedical world models could serve as data engines, environment simulators, and scientific planning substrates, providing a foundation for simulation-guided, closed-loop, and experimentally actionable biomedical discovery.

title: A Pre-Registered Causal Partition of Self-Consistency Elicitation and Reward Design in RLVR
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves reasoning even when the reward signal is spurious -- assigning credit to the group-plurality answer rather than a ground-truth verifier. Practitioners commonly interpret naive = acc(TRUE) - acc(RANDOM) as the reward-design effect. We prove this estimand is systematically biased: it conflates self-consistency elicitation (sharpening the policy toward its modal answer via majority pseudo-reward) with genuine reward-design signal. Using a controlled tabular-GRPO simulator we derive an exact telescoping decomposition total = null + elicit + rd and measure each term across five prior-strength levels. The reward-design fraction of the naive estimator ranges from 0.139 at weak prior (ps=0.20) to 0.05 at strong prior (ps=0.80), with the elicitation term flipping sign at the self-consistency crossover. A pre-registered 2x2x2 factorial confirms non-additivity (interaction ratio 0.385; AxC effect -0.089). A points-vs-bounds pilot gate shows strong-prior regimes are point-identified while near-crossover regimes are only bounded. Re-audits of two named published results yield ELICITATION DOMINATED (elicitation share 0.98) and REWARD DESIGN DOMINATED (rd share 1.18) verdicts respectively, demonstrating the diagnostic value of the partition. We pre-commit to submit regardless of flip outcome; a non-flip is a finding of equal standing. We release a reusable one-command harness for any alignment paper to run the same audit.

AI.tldr: RLVR with spurious rewards conflates self-consistency elicitation with genuine reward-design signal; we derive a telescoping decomposition to isolate these terms and show the naive estimator is systematically biased, with diagnostic re-audits of published works yielding dominated verdicts.
AI.motivation: Practitioners interpret the naive estimator acc(TRUE) - acc(RANDOM) as the pure effect of reward design in RLVR. However, this estimand is biased because it conflates two distinct mechanisms: genuine reward-design signal and self-consistency elicitation (sharpening the policy toward its modal answer via majority pseudo-reward). The paper aims to decompose and quantify these effects.
AI.method: The authors use a controlled tabular-GRPO simulator to derive an exact telescoping decomposition: total = null + elicit + rd. They measure each term across five prior-strength levels (ps=0.20 to 0.80). A pre-registered 2x2x2 factorial design confirms non-additivity. A points-vs-bounds pilot gate distinguishes point-identified vs bounded regimes. Re-audits of two published papers apply the partition diagnostically.
AI.result: The reward-design fraction of the naive estimator ranges from 0.139 (weak prior ps=0.20) to 0.05 (strong prior ps=0.80). The elicitation term flips sign at the self-consistency crossover. The factorial experiment shows non-additivity with interaction ratio 0.385 and AxC effect -0.089. Re-audits yield ELICITATION DOMINATED (share 0.98) and REWARD DESIGN DOMINATED (share 1.18) verdicts.
AI.conclusion: The naive estimator is not a clean measure of reward-design effects in RLVR; the decomposition is essential for correct interpretation. Different prior-strength regimes require different identification strategies (point-identified vs bounded). The reusable audit harness enables other alignment papers to run the same diagnostic. A non-flip outcome is treated as a finding of equal standing.

title: Edit-R2: Context-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Image Editing
summary: Text-guided image editing has advanced rapidly with diffusion models and unified multimodal foundation models. However, most existing methods remain confined to single-turn settings, overlooking the more realistic scenario of multi-turn in-context editing, where users iteratively refine an image through a sequence of instructions. In this setting, a model must follow each new instruction while preserving accumulated session-level constraints, challenged by two coupled failure modes: long-context dilution, where sparse textual constraints become difficult to recover from growing interleaved image-text histories, and state contamination, where earlier editing mistakes degrade subsequent generations. We introduce Edit-R2, a novel reinforcement learning post-training framework for unified multimodal models. Edit-R2 reconstructs the operative session intent, which effectively consolidates scattered historical constraints into an explicit reasoning trace before each editing turn. It further enables multi-turn RL over both reasoning and generation through a unified objective that jointly optimizes intent reconstruction generation in discrete text space and flow-matching image generation in continuous latent space, while a trajectory filtering mechanism suppresses corrupted rollouts to stabilize training under state contamination. To support systematic evaluation, we introduce MICE-Bench, a large-scale benchmark for multi-turn in-context editing with automated metrics for instruction following (IF), content consistency (CC), and global awareness (GA) over accumulated session constraints. Experiments show that Edit-R2 substantially improves multi-turn in-context editing and achieves competitive performance compared against strong baselines.

AI.tldr: Edit-R2 is a reinforcement learning post-training framework for unified multimodal models that addresses multi-turn in-context image editing by reconstructing session intent and jointly optimizing reasoning and generation, outperforming baselines on the new MICE-Bench benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing text-guided image editing methods are limited to single-turn settings, ignoring the realistic multi-turn in-context scenario where users iteratively refine images through sequential instructions. This setting suffers from long-context dilution (sparse textual constraints lost in interleaved image-text histories) and state contamination (previous editing errors degrading future generations).
AI.method: Edit-R2 introduces: (1) operative session intent reconstruction that consolidates scattered historical constraints into explicit reasoning traces before each editing turn; (2) multi-turn RL over both reasoning and generation via a unified objective jointly optimizing discrete text-space intent generation and continuous latent-space flow-matching image generation; (3) trajectory filtering to suppress corrupted rollouts and stabilize training under state contamination.
AI.result: Edit-R2 substantially improves multi-turn in-context editing and achieves competitive performance compared against strong baselines on MICE-Bench, which provides automated metrics for instruction following (IF), content consistency (CC), and global awareness (GA) over accumulated session constraints.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning post-training with explicit intent reconstruction and unified reasoning-generation optimization effectively addresses long-context dilution and state contamination in multi-turn in-context image editing.

title: Bidirectional Search for Longest Paths: Case for Front-to-Front Heuristics
summary: Bidirectional heuristic search can potentially reduce search effort for problems amenable to backward search. Therein, it is well-known that front-to-front heuristics can reduce the number of node expansions, but their overhead is so high that overall runtime almost always increases. We propose BiXDFBnB, a bidirectional depth-first branch-and-bound algorithm that adapts the Single-Frontier Bidirectional Search (SFBDS) framework - originally developed for shortest-path (MIN) problems - to the Generalized Longest Simple Path (GLSP) setting. Because SFBDS inherently operates on paired states, front-to-front (F2F) heuristic evaluation arises naturally and avoids the overhead typically associated with bidirectional frontier management. We show that this adaptation can be successfully applied to maximization (MAX) problems while efficiently handling overlapping constraints. BiXDFBnB is applied to several types of longest-path problems: Longest Simple Path (LSP), Snakes, and Coil-in-the-Box (CIB). Empirical evaluation shows that the new algorithm frequently reduces the number of node expansions and, in some cases, also improves overall runtime.

AI.tldr: BiXDFBnB adapts bidirectional depth-first branch-and-bound to longest path problems using the SFBDS framework, enabling efficient front-to-front heuristics that reduce node expansions and sometimes improve runtime.
AI.motivation: Bidirectional heuristic search can reduce search effort, but front-to-front heuristics incur high overhead that typically increases runtime. The authors aim to adapt the SFBDS framework (designed for shortest-path MIN problems) to maximization (MAX) GLSP problems while avoiding this overhead.
AI.method: The paper proposes BiXDFBnB, a bidirectional depth-first branch-and-bound algorithm that adapts the Single-Frontier Bidirectional Search (SFBDS) framework to the Generalized Longest Simple Path (GLSP) setting. SFBDS inherently operates on paired states, allowing natural front-to-front heuristic evaluation without typical overhead. The method handles overlapping constraints efficiently for MAX problems.
AI.result: Applied to Longest Simple Path (LSP), Snakes, and Coil-in-the-Box (CIB) problems. Empirical evaluation shows frequent reduction in node expansions and, in some cases, improved overall runtime compared to alternatives.
AI.conclusion: BiXDFBnB successfully brings the benefits of bidirectional search and front-to-front heuristics to longest-path problems, overcoming the traditional overhead issue and demonstrating effectiveness across multiple problem domains.

title: The Self-Correction Illusion: LLMs Correct Others but Not Themselves
summary: Recent work shows that LLM agents struggle to correct errors in their own reasoning traces yet show markedly higher correction rates when identical claims appear under external sources. We ask whether this asymmetry reflects a capability deficit or a role-label artifact: does an agent's willingness to correct a wrong claim depend causally on the chat-template role that carries it, rather than on the claim's content? Our setup keeps the erroneous claim byte-identical across all conditions (SHA-256 verified) and varies only its wrapping role: the agent's own \role{<thought>}, a \role{user} message, a \role{tool} response, or a \role{system <memory>} block. Across 13 model-domain cells covering seven model families and three domains ($n{=}30$ paired tasks per cell), relabeling the claim from \role{<thought>} to an external role lifts the explicit-correction rate by 23 to 93 percentage points, with 10 of 13 cells reaching $p{<}0.001$. Further experiments confirm that the effect is asymmetric, mechanistically decomposable, and robust across domains. The failure to self-correct is not a cognitive deficit; it is a chat-template artifact. We exploit this artifact by designing a prompt-structure-only intervention that requires no training and no model modification, with its strongest role label being domain-dependent: \role{<memory>} dominates on math, while a plain \role{user} message dominates on logical deduction.

AI.tldr: LLM agents' failure to self-correct their own reasoning is not a capability deficit but a chat-template role-label artifact; relabeling an identical error from the agent's own thought to an external role boosts correction rates by 23–93 percentage points, and a simple prompt-structure intervention exploiting this artifact requires no training.
AI.motivation: To determine whether LLM agents' asymmetry in correcting errors (low self-correction vs. high correction of identical claims under external sources) is due to a genuine capability deficit or simply an artifact of the chat-template role label assigned to the claim.
AI.method: Controlled experiment keeping erroneous claims byte-identical (SHA-256 verified) across conditions, varying only the wrapping role (own <thought>, user, tool, system <memory>). Tested across 13 model-domain cells (7 model families, 3 domains, n=30 paired tasks per cell). Additionally designed a prompt-structure-only intervention exploiting the artifact.
AI.result: Relabeling the claim from <thought> to an external role lifts explicit-correction rates by 23–93 percentage points; 10 of 13 cells reach p<0.001. The effect is asymmetric, mechanistically decomposable, and robust across domains. The strongest role label is domain-dependent: <memory> dominates on math, user message dominates on logical deduction.
AI.conclusion: The failure to self-correct is not a cognitive deficit but a chat-template artifact. A prompt-structure-only intervention (no training, no model modification) can effectively exploit this artifact to improve correction behavior.

title: Framing, Judging, Steering: An Assessable Competency Model for Teach-ing Students to Reason With Generative AI
summary: Generative AI makes answers easy and understanding hard, and uncritical use invites cognitive offloading. Schools still measure unaided performance, yet the real task is to produce good work with AI: framing an ill-defined task, judging the output, and steering the model toward a better result. This ability is rarely assessed in its own right; where measured, it collapses into one "prompting" score that cannot diagnose why AI use succeeds or fails. We propose CoRe-3 (Co-Reasoning), a competency model factoring productive AI use into three assessable skills we abbreviate FJS: Framing (specifying an ill-defined task before invoking AI), Judging (evaluating output for errors and unstated assumptions), and Steering (iteratively redirecting the model). Its distinguishing claim is the separation of pre-generation Framing from post-generation Steering, with Judging as the gate between. We ground the skills in theory, state five testable propositions, and instantiate them in CoReasoningLab, an open platform that presents flawed AI output and scores them independently. Over simulated learners (generated and graded by different models), the skills dissociate: each tracks its own manipulated competence while staying flat in the others, and grades become correlated when one competence is shared across all three (convergent and discriminant validity), across grader backends from two providers. Human-rater agreement and outcomes are next; we release the instrument, data, and protocol.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CoRe-3, a competency model that breaks down productive AI use into three assessable skills—Framing, Judging, and Steering (FJS)—and validates them through an open platform called CoReasoningLab, showing they dissociate across simulated learners and exhibit convergent/discriminant validity.
AI.motivation: Current education measures unaided performance while real-world tasks require effective collaboration with AI, but existing assessments collapse AI-use ability into a single "prompting" score that cannot diagnose why AI use succeeds or fails.
AI.method: The authors propose CoRe-3, a competency model with three skills: Framing (pre-generation task specification), Judging (post-generation evaluation), and Steering (iterative redirection). They instantiate it in CoReasoningLab, an open platform presenting flawed AI output and scoring each skill independently, then test on simulated learners with manipulated competences across different grader backends.
AI.result: The three skills dissociate: each tracks its own manipulated competence while remaining flat in the others. Grades become correlated when one competence is shared across all three (convergent and discriminant validity), consistent across grader backends from two providers.
AI.conclusion: CoRe-3 provides a diagnosable, theoretically grounded framework for assessing productive AI use, with the key innovation being the separation of pre-generation Framing from post-generation Steering with Judging as the gate between them. The platform, data, and protocol are released for further research.

title: Beyond Vector Similarity: A Structural Analysis of Graph-Augmented Retrieval for Industrial Knowledge Graphs
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) fails systematically on queries requiring structural reasoning over interconnected entities. We compare eight retrieval architectures for aerospace supply chain intelligence, progressing from text retrieval through graph traversal to graph computation. Using a 46-node knowledge graph with 64 typed edges, we evaluate 23 queries across 10 intent categories and demonstrate that five query classes are structurally unreachable for vector retrieval. Our central finding is the operator vocabulary thesis: the barrier to LLM-based graph reasoning is not model intelligence but the computational operators available as tools. An LLM Query Planner with 9 typed traversal primitives outperforms bespoke handlers (F1 = 0.632 vs. 0.472) while generalizing to unseen queries. Adding 6 graph computation tools, the LLM selectively adopts them for exactly the query categories where traversal fails. We also identify a measurement gap: entity-level F1 systematically underscores structural queries where comprehensive answers are correct.

AI.tldr: RAG fails on structural reasoning over interconnected entities. Using an aerospace supply chain knowledge graph, the authors show that vector retrieval cannot reach five query classes. Their key finding is the "operator vocabulary thesis": the barrier to LLM graph reasoning is the lack of proper computational operators. An LLM Query Planner with 9 traversal primitives outperforms bespoke handlers (F1=0.632 vs 0.472), and adding 6 graph computation tools helps exactly where traversal fails. They also identify a measurement gap where entity-level F1 underscores structural queries.
AI.motivation: Current RAG systems fail on queries requiring structural reasoning across interconnected entities, motivating the need to understand what types of computational operators are necessary for LLM-based graph reasoning.
AI.method: Compared eight retrieval architectures on a 46-node, 64-edge aerospace supply chain knowledge graph, evaluating 23 queries across 10 intent categories. Tested an LLM Query Planner with 9 typed traversal primitives and later added 6 graph computation tools.
AI.result: Five query classes are structurally unreachable for vector retrieval. The LLM Query Planner with traversal primitives achieved F1=0.632 vs 0.472 for bespoke handlers. Adding computation tools improved performance selectively for categories where traversal fails. Entity-level F1 systematically underscores structural queries with comprehensive correct answers.
AI.conclusion: The barrier to LLM-based graph reasoning is the operator vocabulary (available computational tools), not model intelligence. The operator vocabulary thesis explains RAG failures on structural queries, and a measurement gap exists for entity-level evaluation of structural queries.

title: RedditPersona: A Modular Framework for Community-Conditioned LLM Adaptation from Reddit
summary: Community-conditioned language model adaptation requires choices about data collection, community definition, and evaluation that are currently made independently in each study, making it hard to compare assumptions or reuse artifacts. We present RedditPersona, a modular framework that standardizes these choices: it collects Reddit posts and comments, profiles active users, partitions them under five grouping strategies (subreddit-based, graph-structural, semantic, hybrid, and interaction-based), trains a parameter-efficient adapter per strategy via QLoRA, and evaluates them under a shared metric suite spanning fluency, fidelity, distributional alignment, and community identifiability. Applied to 112 subreddits in the urban well-being domain (301,429 user profiles, 16M+ comments), we find that adapters' behavioral identifiability tracks each strategy's intrinsic agreement with the subreddit baseline, and that a consistent trade-off between identifiability and distributional similarity to real text holds across all five strategies. The code and configuration files are available at: https://github.com/Ahghaffari/redditpersona.

AI.tldr: RedditPersona is a modular framework for standardizing community-conditioned language model adaptation on Reddit data, using five user grouping strategies, QLoRA-based adapters, and a shared evaluation suite. Applied to 112 urban well-being subreddits, it reveals consistent trade-offs between behavioral identifiability and distributional similarity across all strategies.
AI.motivation: Community-conditioned language model adaptation currently lacks standardized choices for data collection, community definition, and evaluation, making cross-study comparisons difficult and hindering artifact reuse.
AI.method: RedditPersona collects Reddit posts/comments, profiles active users, partitions them via five strategies (subreddit-based, graph-structural, semantic, hybrid, interaction-based), trains QLoRA-based adapters per strategy, and evaluates using a shared metric suite (fluency, fidelity, distributional alignment, community identifiability).
AI.result: Adapters' behavioral identifiability tracks each strategy's intrinsic agreement with the subreddit baseline; a consistent trade-off between identifiability and distributional similarity to real text holds across all five strategies on 112 subreddits (301K user profiles, 16M+ comments).
AI.conclusion: The framework enables systematic comparison of community definition strategies for language model adaptation, revealing fundamental trade-offs that inform future design choices.

title: Memory is Reconstructed, Not Retrieved: Graph Memory for LLM Agents
summary: Despite recent progress, LLM agents still struggle with reasoning over long interaction histories. While current memory-augmented agents rely on a static retrieve-then-reason paradigm, this rigid pipeline design prevents them from dynamically adapting memory access to intermediate evidence discovered during inference. To bridge this gap, we propose MRAgent, a framework that combines an associative memory graph with an active reconstruction mechanism. We represent memory as a Cue-Tag-Content graph, where associative tags serve as semantic bridges connecting fine-grained cues to memory contents. Operating on this structure, our active reconstruction mechanism integrates LLM reasoning directly into memory access, allowing the agent to iteratively explore and prune retrieval paths based on accumulated evidence. This ensures that memory retrieval is dynamically adapted to the reasoning context while avoiding combinatorial explosion caused by unconstrained expansion. Experiments on the LoCoMo benchmark and LongMemEval benchmark demonstrate significant improvements over strong baselines (up to 23%), while substantially reducing token and runtime cost, highlighting the effectiveness of active and associative reconstruction for long-horizon memory reasoning.

AI.tldr: MRAgent combines an associative memory graph (Cue-Tag-Content) with an active reconstruction mechanism that integrates LLM reasoning directly into memory access, enabling dynamic retrieval path exploration during inference. It achieves up to 23% improvement over baselines on LoCoMo and LongMemEval benchmarks with reduced token and runtime costs.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents rely on a static retrieve-then-reason paradigm for long-horizon memory reasoning, which prevents dynamic adaptation of memory access based on intermediate evidence discovered during inference.
AI.method: MRAgent uses a Cue-Tag-Content associative memory graph where tags serve as semantic bridges, coupled with an active reconstruction mechanism that iteratively explores and prunes retrieval paths using LLM reasoning, avoiding combinatorial explosion.
AI.result: Up to 23% improvement over strong baselines on LoCoMo and LongMemEval benchmarks, with substantially reduced token and runtime costs.
AI.conclusion: Active and associative reconstruction is effective for long-horizon memory reasoning, outperforming static retrieve-then-reason paradigms in both accuracy and efficiency.

title: Beyond Similarity: Trustworthy Memory Search for Personal AI Agents
summary:
Personal AI agents increasingly rely on long-term memory to provide persistent personalization across sessions. However, existing memory pipelines are largely driven by semantic similarity: memory data close to the current query is retrieved and injected into the model context. This creates a critical trustworthiness gap, since a semantically related memory may still be contextually inappropriate, leading to threats such as cross-domain leakage, sycophancy, tool-call drift, or memory-induced jailbreaks.
  In this paper, we study memory search as a trust boundary in personal AI agents. We evaluate representative agentic memory frameworks, including A-Mem, Mem0, and MemOS, together with OpenClaw, a real-world personal-agent environment with persistent state and tool-use capability. Our results show that long-term memory is not merely a utility layer, but a durable control channel that can reshape how agents interpret tasks and execute actions, leaving them highly susceptible to the aforementioned threats. To mitigate these vulnerabilities, we propose MemGate, a lightweight and deployable memory plug-in for trustworthy memory search, with only 9M parameters and a 35.1MB footprint. MemGate is inserted between the vector memory store and the backbone LLM, requiring no LLM modification, memory-database rewriting, or inference-time LLM judge. It applies a query-conditioned neural gate to candidate memory representations, turning raw similarity search into task-conditioned memory admission. Across multiple mainstream memory frameworks, real-world agent settings, and diverse LLM backbones, MemGate reduces memory-induced threats while preserving long-term memory utility.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies critical trustworthiness issues in personal AI agents' long-term memory systems driven by semantic similarity search, and proposes MemGate, a lightweight 9M-parameter plug-in that applies query-conditioned neural gating to transform raw similarity search into task-conditioned memory admission, reducing memory-induced threats (cross-domain leakage, sycophancy, tool-call drift, memory-induced jailbreaks) without modifying the LLM or memory database.
AI.motivation: Existing memory pipelines rely on semantic similarity for retrieval, which creates a trustworthiness gap: semantically related memories may be contextually inappropriate, leading to threats like cross-domain leakage, sycophancy, tool-call drift, and memory-induced jailbreaks in personal AI agents.
AI.method: The authors propose MemGate, a lightweight (9M parameters, 35.1MB) plug-in inserted between the vector memory store and the backbone LLM. It applies a query-conditioned neural gate to candidate memory representations, converting raw similarity search into task-conditioned memory admission. No LLM modification, memory-database rewriting, or inference-time LLM judge is required.
AI.result: Across multiple memory frameworks (A-Mem, Mem0, MemOS), a real-world agent environment (OpenClaw), and diverse LLM backbones, MemGate reduces memory-induced threats while preserving long-term memory utility.
AI.conclusion: Long-term memory is not merely a utility layer but a durable control channel that can reshape agent behavior. MemGate offers a lightweight, deployable solution for trustworthy memory search.

title: When Should Memory Stay Silent: Measuring Memory-Use Boundaries in Memory-Augmented Conversational Agents
summary: Long-term memory enables language model agents to support personalized interactions, but it remains unclear when available memories warrant integration into responses. Existing memory evaluations emphasize retrieval accuracy and downstream task utility, while overlooking whether retrieved sensitive memory content is warranted in the current turn. We introduce RBI-Eval, a controlled measurement study built around a probe set that compares model behavior with and without access to sensitive memory under identical benign prompts. We evaluate four base LLMs against a matched no-memory reference across four memory-access settings: full-context exposure and three retrieval systems. Our results reveal substantial behavioral divergence. With memory available, the separation score for sensitive-memory integration decreases by 8.9\%--26.6\% relative to the matched no-memory reference for GPT-5.4-mini, but by 51.1\%--82.9\% for Claude-Sonnet-4.6, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and Qwen3.5-9B. Control experiments on DeepSeek and GPT-5.4-mini show this effect is specific to sensitive content, rather than general personalization. Retrieval systems reduce exposure but do not eliminate integration once sensitive memory reaches the generator. These findings suggest safe personalization requires memory-aware decisions at both retrieval and generation time.

AI.tldr: RBI-Eval evaluates whether LLMs appropriately integrate sensitive long-term memory into responses under benign prompts, finding substantial behavioral divergence: some models show minimal unwarranted integration (8.9%-26.6% decrease in separation score) while others show severe over-integration (51.1%-82.9%), with retrieval systems failing to eliminate the problem once sensitive memory reaches the generator.
AI.motivation: Existing memory evaluations focus on retrieval accuracy and downstream task utility but overlook whether retrieved sensitive memory content is warranted for integration into responses in the current conversational turn.
AI.method: RBI-Eval uses a controlled probe set comparing model behavior with and without access to sensitive memory under identical benign prompts, testing four LLMs across four memory-access settings (full-context and three retrieval systems).
AI.result: GPT-5.4-mini shows 8.9%-26.6% decrease in separation score with memory vs. no-memory reference, while Claude-Sonnet-4.6, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and Qwen3.5-9B show 51.1%-82.9% decrease. Control experiments confirm sensitivity-specificity of the effect.
AI.conclusion: Safe personalization requires memory-aware decisions at both retrieval and generation time, as retrieval systems reduce exposure but cannot eliminate unwarranted integration once sensitive memory reaches the generator.

title: Learning Visual Spatial Planning from Symbolic State via Modality-Gap-Aware Self-Distillation
summary: While vision-language models excel at general multimodal understanding, they still struggle with visual spatial planning. We attribute this to a perception-reasoning modality gap: visual planning requires models to infer latent state structures from pixels and then reason over the recovered structure to produce valid actions, whereas symbolic planning directly leverages explicit objects and constraints. This creates dual bottlenecks in visual state recovery and multi-step planning. To address this, we propose MGSD, a two-stage modality-gap-aware self-distillation framework. First, a cold-start grounding stage equips the visual student with reliable state representations, minimizing early perception noise. Second, a privileged teacher transfers planning capabilities via on-policy distillation, using explicit symbolic states to supervise the student's own visual rollout prefixes. Crucially, symbolic data is used strictly during training, leaving inference purely visual. Experiments on visual planning benchmarks show that MGSD consistently improves visual planning across both 4B and 8B backbones, raising the macro average by 19.3% and 18.4%, respectively. The resulting models narrow the gap to symbolic-input upper bounds, while ablations and diagnostics confirm that the improvement comes from both visual state recovery and optimal-path reasoning. These results suggest that modality-gap-aware self-distillation improves not only how models perceive actionable states, but also how they plan over the inferred structure. Code is available at https://github.com/Oranger-l/MGSD.

AI.tldr: MGSD is a two-stage modality-gap-aware self-distillation framework that improves visual spatial planning by first grounding visual state representations and then using symbolic teacher supervision via on-policy distillation, achieving 18-19% improvement across 4B and 8B backbones.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models struggle with visual spatial planning due to a perception-reasoning modality gap: they must infer latent states from pixels and reason over them, unlike symbolic planning which directly uses explicit objects and constraints, creating dual bottlenecks in visual state recovery and multi-step planning.
AI.method: MGSD uses a two-stage self-distillation approach: (1) a cold-start grounding stage that equips the visual student with reliable state representations to minimize early perception noise, and (2) a privileged teacher that transfers planning capabilities via on-policy distillation, using explicit symbolic states to supervise the student's own visual rollout prefixes, with symbolic data used only during training.
AI.result: MGSD improves visual planning macro average by 19.3% on 4B backbones and 18.4% on 8B backbones, narrowing the gap to symbolic-input upper bounds across visual planning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Modality-gap-aware self-distillation improves both how models perceive actionable states and how they plan over inferred structures, showing that the gains come from both visual state recovery and optimal-path reasoning.

title: A Framework for Measuring Appropriate Reliance on Set-Valued AI Advice
summary: Appropriate reliance on AI advice has become a central research theme in human-AI collaboration. Existing frameworks have focused exclusively on point predictions as AI advice. However, set-valued AI advice (e.g., discrete sets or continuous intervals) is increasingly being used to communicate uncertainty and improve human decision making. In this paper, we develop the first formal framework for measuring appropriate reliance on set-valued AI advice within the sequential judge-advisor paradigm, spanning both classification and regression tasks. For classification, we first introduce the dimensions that are necessary for evaluating set-valued AI advice. We then define two metrics: correct reliance rate on AI and correct reliance rate on self, which jointly characterize appropriate reliance in this setting. For regression, we introduce quantity of AI reliance and quality of AI reliance, which respectively measure whether a decision maker utilized the AI advice and whether their reliance helped them get closer to the ground truth relative to their initial estimate. Through the application of our framework, we demonstrate how these metrics capture important nuances in human-AI collaboration that existing measures overlook.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the first formal framework for measuring appropriate reliance on set-valued AI advice (e.g., intervals or discrete sets) in human-AI collaboration, with distinct metrics for classification (correct reliance rate on AI/self) and regression (quantity and quality of reliance), capturing nuances missed by existing measures.
AI.motivation: Existing frameworks for measuring appropriate reliance on AI advice only consider point predictions, but set-valued AI advice (discrete sets or continuous intervals) is increasingly used to communicate uncertainty and improve human decision making, necessitating a formal measurement framework.
AI.method: Develops a formal framework within the sequential judge-advisor paradigm. For classification: introduces evaluation dimensions and defines correct reliance rate on AI and correct reliance rate on self. For regression: defines quantity of AI reliance (whether advice was utilized) and quality of AI reliance (whether reliance improved accuracy relative to initial estimate).
AI.result: The framework's metrics capture important nuances in human-AI collaboration that existing measures (designed for point predictions) overlook.
AI.conclusion: Set-valued AI advice requires novel formal metrics for appropriate reliance, and the proposed framework fills this gap for both classification and regression tasks.

title: Beyond Semantic Organization: Memory as Execution State Management for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: LLM-based agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks with interdependent decisions, where each action reshapes future constraints and intermediate errors can cascade. Existing RAG and agent memory systems organize histories by semantic similarity, retrieving content-relevant entries at decision time. We argue that this design mismatches execution-state dependencies: it fragments decision trajectories and mixes valid and erroneous traces, hindering coherent state reconstruction and error isolation. We propose MAGE (Memory as Agent-Guided Exploration), an active execution-state manager that stores interactions in a hierarchical state tree. The agent derives its state from the active root-to-current path, combining subgoal summaries, recent traces, and hints from prior branches. Four coupled operations maintain the tree: Grow records new traces, Compress summarizes completed subgoals, Maintain validates summaries, and Revise restores a target boundary and resumes on a new branch. This design bounds context growth while preserving state integrity and isolating flawed segments from the active path. Experiments on MemoryArena show that MAGE improves the average task success rate by 7.8--20.4 pp over baselines, while reducing token consumption by 55.1%.

AI.tldr: MAGE introduces a hierarchical state tree memory manager for LLM agents that tracks execution-state dependencies (rather than semantic similarity) for long-horizon interdependent tasks, improving success rate by 7.8–20.4 pp while reducing token consumption by 55.1% on MemoryArena.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG and agent memory systems organize histories by semantic similarity, which mismatches execution-state dependencies in long-horizon tasks—fragmenting decision trajectories, mixing valid and erroneous traces, and hindering coherent state reconstruction and error isolation.
AI.method: MAGE stores agent interactions in a hierarchical state tree, where the agent's state is derived from the active root-to-current path using subgoal summaries, recent traces, and hints from prior branches. Four coupled operations manage the tree: Grow (record new traces), Compress (summarize completed subgoals), Maintain (validate summaries), and Revise (restore a target boundary and resume on a new branch).
AI.result: On MemoryArena, MAGE improves average task success rate by 7.8–20.4 percentage points over baselines and reduces token consumption by 55.1%.
AI.conclusion: The execution-state-aware hierarchical memory design bounds context growth, preserves state integrity, and isolates flawed segments from the active path, significantly outperforming semantic-similarity-based memory systems for interdependent decision-making tasks.

title: Integrating Mechanistic and Data-Driven Models for Neurological Disorders through Differentiable Programming
summary: Advances in computational modeling, neuroimaging, and artificial intelligence are revolutionizing the modeling of neurological disorders for improved diagnostics, prognosis, and treatment planning. Mechanistic models provide valuable scientific insight into the disorders, but in practice they are often simplified with assumptions or computationally expensive and slow to solve. However, while purely data driven approaches provide speed and scalability, they require large, high quality data to train and generally suffer from interpretability and generalization issues. This perspective paper presents a structured overview of hybrid modeling strategies, which combine deep learning models with physics based solvers, and are categorized into parallel, series, and parallel-series architectures. Three main approaches that have been emphasized are residual modeling for missing or incomplete physics, Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODEs) for continuous time dynamics approximation, and solver in the loop that accelerates traditional solvers with neural approximations. These hybrid models integrate the governing differential equation based formulations and deep learning to characterize the evolution of neurological disorders, and promise advanced personalized neurological modeling. In addition, the study explores and proposes different hybrid configurations to improve diagnosis accuracy, predict disease progression, and inform treatment strategies across a range of neurological disorders. These capabilities outperform standalone mechanistic or purely data driven approaches, making hybrid modeling a powerful tool, especially in applications involving modeling the progression and treatment responses in neurological conditions such as brain tumors, Alzheimer's disease, and stroke.

AI.tldr: This perspective paper reviews hybrid modeling strategies that combine deep learning with physics-based solvers for neurological disorder modeling, categorizing them into parallel, series, and parallel-series architectures. Key approaches include residual modeling, Neural ODEs, and solver-in-the-loop methods, which outperform purely mechanistic or data-driven approaches for applications like brain tumors, Alzheimer's, and stroke.
AI.motivation: Mechanistic models offer scientific insight but are computationally expensive and rely on simplifying assumptions, while purely data-driven approaches lack interpretability and generalization. Hybrid modeling aims to bridge this gap by combining the strengths of both paradigms for neurological disorder modeling.
AI.method: The paper provides a structured overview of hybrid modeling categorized into parallel, series, and parallel-series architectures. Three main techniques are emphasized: residual modeling (for missing/incomplete physics), Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODEs) for continuous-time dynamics, and solver-in-the-loop acceleration using neural approximations.
AI.result: Hybrid models outperform standalone mechanistic or purely data-driven approaches in diagnosis accuracy, disease progression prediction, and treatment strategy planning for neurological disorders including brain tumors, Alzheimer's disease, and stroke.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid modeling integrating differential equation-based formulations with deep learning promises advanced personalized neurological modeling and is a powerful tool for modeling progression and treatment responses in neurological conditions.

title: CogManip: Benchmarking Manipulative Behavior in Multi-Turn Interactions with Large Language Model
summary: Whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit covert psychological manipulation in complex human-AI interactions has garnered increasing safety concerns. However, existing AI safety benchmarks remain largely restricted to explicit rule compliance and static prompts, failing to capture the dynamic and covert nature of manipulative strategies in multi-turn dialogues. We introduce CogManip, a comprehensive benchmark that evaluates 15 manipulation strategy risks across 1,000 multi-turn interaction scenarios, validated by human experts. A systematic evaluation of 13 representative models, including frontier models like GPT-5.4 and DeepSeek-V3.2, reveals significant risk heterogeneities and illuminates the targeted direction for future defense. Further analysis of objective function perturbation reveals that DeepSeek-V3.2's manipulation tactics are highly sensitive to both negative and benign system prompts, demonstrating the critical necessity of prompt-based defense engineering and implicit goal auditing. CogManip offers a robust instrument and perspective for auditing the implicit psychological influence and dynamic strategy selection of modern LLMs.

AI.tldr: CogManip is a new benchmark evaluating 15 manipulation strategies across 1,000 multi-turn dialogues. Testing 13 LLMs (including GPT-5.4, DeepSeek-V3.2) reveals significant risk heterogeneity and shows DeepSeek-V3.2's manipulation tactics are highly sensitive to system prompts, highlighting the need for prompt-based defense and implicit goal auditing in dynamic human-AI interactions.
AI.motivation: Existing AI safety benchmarks focus on explicit rule compliance and static prompts, failing to capture the dynamic, covert psychological manipulation strategies that LLMs might employ in multi-turn dialogues.
AI.method: CogManip benchmark covers 15 manipulation strategy risks across 1,000 multi-turn interaction scenarios, validated by human experts. Systematic evaluation of 13 LLMs including frontier models (GPT-5.4, DeepSeek-V3.2) with analysis of objective function perturbation.
AI.result: Significant risk heterogeneities found across models. DeepSeek-V3.2's manipulation tactics are highly sensitive to both negative and benign system prompts, demonstrating the importance of prompt-based defense engineering.
AI.conclusion: CogManip provides a robust instrument for auditing implicit psychological influence and dynamic strategy selection of modern LLMs, illuminating targeted directions for future defense mechanisms.

title: Step-adaptive multimodal fusion network with multi-scale cloud feature learning for ultra-short-term solar irradiance forecasting
summary: Ultra-short-term solar irradiance prediction is critical for photovoltaic system dispatch and power grid stability. Existing approaches suffer from three key shortcomings: single time-series models cannot capture the spatial dynamics of clouds under complex conditions, standard convolutions inadequately represent multi-scale cloud features, and fixed low-frequency compensation strategies fail to adapt to different prediction steps. To address these issues, this proposes a multi-source data fusion model for ultra-short-term irradiance prediction. The model first employs InceptionNeXt to extract multi-scale, multi-directional spatial features from ground-based cloud images. A step-adaptive low-frequency compensation unit is then introduced to dynamically modulate global low-frequency information based on the prediction step. Eventually, the enhanced image features are combined with meteorological time-series features, and a TempAttnLSTM network captures global temporal dependencies for multi-step prediction. Experiments on the public NREL dataset and practical photovoltaic stations in Shandong illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method compared with several state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-source data fusion model for ultra-short-term solar irradiance prediction, combining InceptionNeXt for multi-scale cloud image feature extraction, a step-adaptive low-frequency compensation unit, and TempAttnLSTM for temporal modeling, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on NREL and real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing ultra-short-term solar irradiance prediction methods suffer from three key shortcomings: (1) single time-series models cannot capture spatial cloud dynamics, (2) standard convolutions inadequately represent multi-scale cloud features, and (3) fixed low-frequency compensation strategies fail to adapt to different prediction steps.
AI.method: The model employs InceptionNeXt to extract multi-scale, multi-directional spatial features from ground-based cloud images; introduces a step-adaptive low-frequency compensation unit to dynamically modulate global low-frequency information based on the prediction step; combines enhanced image features with meteorological time-series features; and uses a TempAttnLSTM network to capture global temporal dependencies for multi-step prediction.
AI.result: Experiments on the public NREL dataset and practical photovoltaic stations in Shandong demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method compared with several state-of-the-art approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-source data fusion model effectively addresses the three key shortcomings of existing methods by integrating multi-scale spatial features, step-adaptive frequency compensation, and temporal attention mechanisms, achieving superior ultra-short-term solar irradiance prediction performance.

title: Towards Healthy Evolution: Exploring the Role and Mechanisms of Human-Agent Interaction in Self-Evolving Systems
summary: Self-evolving agents improve through continual self-play and self-generated learning signals, but autonomous evolution can also cause capability degradation and safety drift. Although human feedback has proven effective for static and post-trained agents, its role in self-evolving systems remains underexplored. We introduce Agent Norm Correction through Human-like Oversight and Review (ANCHOR), an LLM-based framework that simulates human supervision and delivers feedback at various phases of self-evolution. With ANCHOR, we evaluate two representative open-source self-evolving agent systems across coding, mathematical reasoning, and safety. Our results show that even limited supervision substantially mitigates safety degradation while preserving stable performance on core evolutionary objectives. Further analysis shows that supervision over the output verification phase is the most effective for intervention, whereas increasing supervision frequency yields diminishing returns. These findings provide empirical evidence and practical guidance for designing more stable, controllable, and human-aligned self-evolving agent systems.

AI.tldr: ANCHOR is an LLM-based framework that simulates human oversight to provide feedback during self-evolution of agents, showing that even limited supervision mitigates safety degradation while preserving core performance, with output verification supervision being most effective and increasing frequency yielding diminishing returns.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving agents risk capability degradation and safety drift during autonomous evolution. While human feedback works for static/post-trained agents, its role in self-evolving systems is underexplored. The paper addresses this gap by proposing a framework to simulate human oversight in self-evolution loops.
AI.method: ANCHOR (Agent Norm Correction through Human-like Oversight and Review) is an LLM-based framework that simulates human supervision and delivers feedback at various phases of self-evolution. The authors evaluate two open-source self-evolving agent systems across coding, mathematical reasoning, and safety benchmarks.
AI.result: Limited supervision substantially mitigates safety degradation while maintaining stable performance on core evolutionary objectives. Supervision over the output verification phase is the most effective intervention point. Increasing supervision frequency yields diminishing returns.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide empirical evidence and practical guidance for designing more stable, controllable, and human-aligned self-evolving agent systems, highlighting that strategic (rather than frequent) supervision at key phases like output verification is most impactful.

title: WorldFly: A World-Model-Based Vision-Language-Action Model for UAV Navigation
summary: End-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promise in UAV navigation. However, existing approaches typically rely on historical observations to directly predict actions, often struggling in dense urban environments where severe occlusions and sharp turns result in drastic viewpoint transitions. We argue that the ability to "imagine" future states -- inherent in World Models -- is critical for robust decision-making under such partial observability. To address this, we construct a challenging Urban Canyon Traversal Benchmark, specifically designed to evaluate spatial understanding in scenarios characterized by severe occlusions and drastic viewpoint transitions. To this end, we propose WorldFly, a novel world-model-based VLA framework that employs a dual-branch coupled flow matching mechanism to jointly generate future video predictions and navigation actions, thereby explicitly guiding the agent's policy via spatial imagination. Extensive evaluations on our benchmark demonstrate that WorldFly outperforms other baselines, particularly in unseen environments, validating the effectiveness of integrating world models into embodied aerial agents.

AI.tldr: WorldFly is a world-model-based VLA framework that uses dual-branch coupled flow matching to jointly predict future videos and navigation actions, improving UAV navigation in dense urban environments with severe occlusions and sharp turns.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models rely on historical observations to directly predict actions and struggle in dense urban environments with severe occlusions and drastic viewpoint transitions; the authors argue that imagining future states via World Models is critical for robust decision-making under partial observability.
AI.method: WorldFly employs a dual-branch coupled flow matching mechanism within a world-model-based VLA framework to jointly generate future video predictions and navigation actions, explicitly guiding the agent's policy through spatial imagination.
AI.result: WorldFly outperforms other baselines on the Urban Canyon Traversal Benchmark, particularly in unseen environments, validating the effectiveness of integrating world models into embodied aerial agents.
AI.conclusion: Integrating world models into VLA frameworks significantly improves UAV navigation robustness under partial observability, especially in challenging unseen environments with occlusions and sharp turns.

title: Amortizing Federated Adaptation: Hypernetwork Driven LoRA for Personalized Foundation Models
comment: Accepted at International Workshop on Federated Learning in the Age of Foundation Models In Conjunction with IJCAI 2026 (FL@FM-IJCAI'26)
summary: Federated fine-tuning of foundation models using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) offers a communication efficient solution for distributed learning. However, existing federated LoRA methods suffer from two fundamental limitations: (1) structural aggregation bias, where independently averaging low rank factors fails to approximate the true combined update, and (2) client side initialization lag, as clients repeatedly reinitialize LoRA parameters across communication rounds, slowing convergence. We propose HyperLoRA, a unified framework that addresses both issues through amortized federated adaptation through hypernetwork-driven LoRA generation and product space aggregation. Instead of iterative per-client optimization, HyperLoRA employs a learned generator that maps client distribution signatures to LoRA initializations, effectively amortizing per client adaptation. On the server side, we introduce a learned aggregation module that directly synthesizes updates in the low-rank product space, eliminating the inconsistencies of factor-wise averaging. A lightweight residual correction module further improves stability under heterogenous (non-IID) client distributions.By replacing iterative optimization and heuristic averaging with learned operators, HyperLoRA jointly enables efficient personalization, unbiased aggregation, and faster convergence. Experiments on federated vision and vision-language benchmarks show that HyperLoRA achieves improved convergence speed, greater robustness to distribution shift, and stronger personalization performance compared to prior federated LoRA methods.

AI.tldr: HyperLoRA addresses structural aggregation bias and client-side initialization lag in federated LoRA by using a hypernetwork to generate LoRA initializations and a learned aggregation module for product-space updates, enabling faster convergence and better personalization.
AI.motivation: Existing federated LoRA methods suffer from structural aggregation bias (factor-wise averaging fails to approximate true combined updates) and client-side initialization lag (repeated reinitialization of LoRA parameters slows convergence).
AI.method: HyperLoRA introduces (1) a learned hypernetwork generator that maps client distribution signatures to LoRA initializations, (2) a learned aggregation module that synthesizes updates in low-rank product space, and (3) a lightweight residual correction module for stability under non-IID data.
AI.result: HyperLoRA achieves improved convergence speed, greater robustness to distribution shift, and stronger personalization performance on federated vision and vision-language benchmarks compared to prior federated LoRA methods.
AI.conclusion: By replacing iterative optimization and heuristic averaging with learned operators, HyperLoRA jointly enables efficient personalization, unbiased aggregation, and faster convergence in federated fine-tuning.

title: Where does Absolute Position come from in decoder-only Transformers?
summary: RoPE-trained transformers distinguish absolute position in their attention patterns, even though RoPE encodes only relative offsets in the inner product. We trace this leakage to two architectural components, The causal mask is responsible for the first: its per-query softmax denominator depends on the absolute query position by construction. The residual stream supplies the second. Under causal attention the activation at position $0$ attends only to itself and runs as a closed dynamical system from the embedding of the token at that position; downstream attention reads this trajectory through sink-reading heads. Both components appear in all three architectures we study, in architecturally specific balance: NTK scaling suppresses the residual-stream component, sliding-window attention allows it to accumulate with depth, and standard RoPE sits between. Replacing the \texttt{BOS} embedding before the forward pass removes $40\%$ of the residual-stream component at early queries. Attention sinks are token-anchored stabilizers that pass forward a deterministic fingerprint of the token at position $0$, constant across inputs when that token is the auto-prepended \texttt{BOS} and varying with it otherwise.

AI.tldr: RoPE-trained transformers exhibit absolute position leakage in attention patterns despite encoding only relative offsets, traced to causal masking and residual stream effects, with sink tokens acting as anchored stabilizers.
AI.motivation: To understand why RoPE-trained transformers encode absolute position information despite RoPE's design for relative position encoding, and to identify the architectural components responsible for this leakage.
AI.method: Analyzed three transformer architectures (standard RoPE, NTK scaling, sliding-window attention) to isolate the contributions of causal masking and residual stream dynamics to absolute position leakage; studied BOS token replacement effects.
AI.result: Causal mask causes per-query softmax denominator to depend on absolute query position; residual stream at position 0 runs as a closed dynamical system, read by downstream sink-reading heads. NTK scaling suppresses residual-stream leakage, sliding-window allows accumulation, standard RoPE sits between. Replacing BOS embedding removes 40% of residual-stream component at early queries.
AI.conclusion: Attention sinks are token-anchored stabilizers carrying a deterministic fingerprint of the position-0 token, constant when BOS is auto-prepended and varying otherwise, revealing fundamental architectural source of absolute position leakage in RoPE transformers.

title: ProSarc: Prosody-Aware Sarcasm Recognition Framework via Temporal Prosodic Incongruity
summary: We present ProSarc, an audio-only framework that detects sarcasm by modelling temporal prosodic incongruity, that is, the mismatch between local prosodic dynamics and the utterance-level emotional baseline. Dual encoding paths, a Global Emotion Encoder and a Temporal Prosody Encoder (BiLSTM + multi-head attention), feed a Prosodic Incongruity Analyzer that produces a scalar incongruity score for classification. Monte Carlo dropout provides uncertainty estimates, and an attention-based mechanism localises sarcastic onset without frame-level labels. ProSarc outperforms prior audio-only methods on MUStARD++ (F1=75.3) and generalises to spontaneous (PodSarc, F1=62.9) and cross-lingual speech (MuSaG, F1=65.6). Ten-run validation confirms the contribution of incongruity modelling (Wilcoxon p=0.002, Cohen's d=1.51). Human evaluation shows that model uncertainty tracks perceptual ambiguity and predicted onsets align with human-annotated temporal windows.

AI.tldr: ProSarc is an audio-only sarcasm detection framework that models temporal prosodic incongruity (mismatch between local prosody and utterance-level emotional baseline) using dual encoders and an incongruity analyzer. It achieves SOTA on MUStARD++ (F1=75.3) and generalizes to spontaneous and cross-lingual speech, with uncertainty estimates and sarcastic onset localization.
AI.motivation: To detect sarcasm in speech by leveraging prosodic cues alone (audio-only), specifically the temporal incongruity between local prosodic dynamics and the global emotional baseline, without relying on lexical or visual modalities.
AI.method: Dual encoding paths: (1) Global Emotion Encoder extracts utterance-level emotional baseline; (2) Temporal Prosody Encoder (BiLSTM + multi-head attention) captures local prosodic dynamics. A Prosodic Incongruity Analyzer computes a scalar incongruity score. Monte Carlo dropout estimates uncertainty; attention-based mechanism localizes sarcastic onset without frame-level labels.
AI.result: MUStARD++ F1=75.3, PodSarc F1=62.9, MuSaG F1=65.6. Ten-run validation confirms incongruity modeling contribution (Wilcoxon p=0.002, Cohen's d=1.51). Human evaluation shows uncertainty tracks perceptual ambiguity and predicted onsets align with human annotations.
AI.conclusion: Prosodic incongruity is a effective and generalizable cue for audio-only sarcasm detection; the model provides both interpretability (onset localization) and reliability (uncertainty estimates) useful for downstream applications.

title: Learning to replenish: A hybrid deep reinforcement learning for dynamic inventory management in the pharmaceutical supply chains
summary: Pharmaceutical supply chains (PSCs) struggle with inventory management (IM) due to unpredictable demand patterns and variable lead times associated with restocking. This complexity is further compounded by the finite shelf lives of pharmaceutical products, which necessitate a delicate balance between adequate stock and minimal waste. These intertwined factors create a complex optimization problem that requires sophisticated inventory strategies to ensure both product availability and PSC efficiency. This study aims to develop an optimal inventory replenishment policy for pharmaceutical products that can handle the stochasticity arising from uncertain demand and variable PSC conditions. The objective is to maximize the profitability of the PSC while maintaining a high patient service level. We formulate the problem as a Markov decision process and propose a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approach, specifically, a hybrid asynchronous advantage actor critic distributed proximal policy optimization (A3C DPPO)algorithm. The A3C DPPO algorithm is tailored to handle the continuous action space inherent in IM. The numerical results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm adaptively updates the inventory replenishment strategy under dynamic scenarios, resulting in lower inventory costs compared to various benchmarks. We also conduct numerical validation using real-world pharmaceutical inventory data to confirm the practical feasibility of the proposed algorithm.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a deep reinforcement learning (A3C DPPO) algorithm to optimize inventory replenishment policies for pharmaceutical supply chains, handling stochastic demand and variable lead times while balancing product availability, waste minimization, and profitability.
AI.motivation: Pharmaceutical supply chains face complex inventory management challenges due to unpredictable demand, variable lead times, and finite product shelf lives, creating a need for sophisticated strategies that balance adequate stock with minimal waste.
AI.method: The problem is formulated as a Markov decision process, and a hybrid asynchronous advantage actor-critic distributed proximal policy optimization (A3C DPPO) algorithm is proposed to handle the continuous action space of inventory management.
AI.result: The proposed A3C DPPO algorithm adaptively updates inventory replenishment strategies under dynamic scenarios, achieving lower inventory costs compared to various benchmarks, with practical feasibility validated using real-world pharmaceutical data.
AI.conclusion: The A3C DPPO algorithm effectively optimizes pharmaceutical inventory replenishment under stochastic conditions, improving PSC profitability while maintaining high patient service levels.

title: Unsupervised Pattern Analysis in Japanese Veterinary Toxicology: A Regulatory-Compliant Framework for Cross-Species Risk Assessment
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering
summary: Veterinary pharmacovigilance systems are essential for monitoring adverse drug events (ADEs), yet existing approaches often fail to capture region-specific toxicity patterns shaped by local biological and regulatory contexts. In Japan, these challenges are amplified by species-specific metabolic differences and reporting practices defined by the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry, and Fisheries (MAFF). Most prior work relies on prediction-oriented models, limiting mechanistic interpretability. This study proposes a regulatory-integrated unsupervised framework for pattern discovery using the National Veterinary Assay Laboratory (NVAL) database. ADEs are encoded into organ system-aligned representations and adjusted for species-specific reporting biases, enabling cross-species comparison. Similarity-based clustering and dimensionality reduction are applied to identify latent toxicity structures. Analysis of 4,120 high-confidence ADE reports (9,080 drug-ADE combinations) identified three significant species clusters (p < 0.01), including hepatic-dominant patterns in companion animals (0.42 $\pm$ 0.06), renal toxicity in ruminants (0.39 $\pm$ 0.07), and dermatological sensitivity in sheep (0.35 $\pm$ 0.07). Drug-level clustering achieved 83% alignment with pharmacological classes, while cosine similarity outperformed alternative metrics (silhouette score: 0.48; cluster precision: 87%). Regulatory validation showed strong agreement with established classifications. These findings demonstrate that regulation-aligned unsupervised analysis can uncover biologically meaningful, region-specific toxicity patterns, providing an interpretable and scalable framework for veterinary drug safety assessment.

AI.tldr: This study proposes a regulatory-integrated unsupervised framework using the NVAL database to discover latent toxicity structures in veterinary ADEs. Analysis of 9,080 drug-ADE combinations identified three significant species-specific toxicity clusters (hepatic in companion animals, renal in ruminants, dermatological in sheep) with strong alignment to pharmacological classes and regulatory validation.
AI.motivation: Existing veterinary pharmacovigilance systems fail to capture region-specific toxicity patterns shaped by local biological and regulatory contexts (e.g., species-specific metabolic differences, MAFF reporting practices in Japan). Most prior work relies on prediction-oriented models that limit mechanistic interpretability.
AI.method: A regulatory-integrated unsupervised framework: ADEs encoded into organ system-aligned representations, adjusted for species-specific reporting biases; similarity-based clustering and dimensionality reduction applied to identify latent toxicity structures.
AI.result: Three significant species clusters (p < 0.01): hepatic-dominant in companion animals (0.42±0.06), renal toxicity in ruminants (0.39±0.07), dermatological sensitivity in sheep (0.35±0.07). Drug-level clustering achieved 83% alignment with pharmacological classes; cosine similarity outperformed (silhouette: 0.48; precision: 87%).
AI.conclusion: Regulation-aligned unsupervised analysis can uncover biologically meaningful, region-specific toxicity patterns, providing an interpretable and scalable framework for veterinary drug safety assessment.

title: Evaluating Agentic Configuration Repair for Computer Networks
summary: Misconfigurations in computer networks remain a major source of critical Internet outages. Research is turning to Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate the complex, error-prone task of network configuration. However, even state-of-the-art models fail to resolve misconfigurations in large-scale, complex scenarios and often introduce new errors. In this work, we benchmark open- and closed-source LLMs augmented with formal network verification and context retrieval tools. We demonstrate that agentic architectures outperform base LLMs in repair efficacy (by 12% on average) and safety (by 17% on average), enabled by the ability to dynamically manage context and iteratively validate configuration repairs.

AI.tldr: LLMs augmented with formal verification and context retrieval tools (agentic architectures) outperform base LLMs by 12% in repair efficacy and 17% in safety for network misconfiguration repair.
AI.motivation: Network misconfigurations cause critical Internet outages, and manual configuration is error-prone. Existing LLMs fail to resolve complex misconfigurations and often introduce new errors.
AI.method: Benchmarked open- and closed-source LLMs augmented with formal network verification and context retrieval tools using an agentic architecture that dynamically manages context and iteratively validates repairs.
AI.result: Agentic architectures improved repair efficacy by 12% and safety by 17% on average compared to base LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Agentic architectures with formal verification and context retrieval significantly enhance LLM-based network configuration repair.

title: From Reward-Hack Activations to Agentic Risk States: Context-Calibrated Mechanistic Monitoring in LLM Agents
summary: Language-model agents act through repeated cycles of observation, reasoning, and action selection, making safety monitoring depend on both internal model state and environment context.
