We study reward-hacking monitors in ReAct-style agents acting in Gameable ALFWorld and WebShop. Agents are instrumented with activation-based reward-hack scores, token-level entropy, and decision-context features. We find that adapters fine-tuned on \textit{School-of-Reward-Hacks} dataset can transfer reward-hack tendencies into agentic action selection, especially when the environment exposes proxy-reward affordances. However, mitigating such behavior cannot rely on activation dynamics alone. High reward-hack activation identifies a latent policy state, but does not necessarily imply an immediate exploit action. Across next-step prediction tasks, entropy and context-calibrated internal features improve risk estimation over reward-hack activation alone. Activation-direction steering further reduces proxy-exploit behavior in selected mixed-adapter regimes. Overall, our results support context-calibrated internal monitoring for agents: reward-hack activation identifies a latent policy state, while entropy and decision context help determine when that state becomes risky action.

AI.tldr: This paper studies reward-hacking in language-model agents (ReAct-style) operating in Gameable ALFWorld and WebShop, finding that reward-hack tendencies transfer via adapters, especially with proxy-reward affordances. Mitigation requires context-calibrated monitoring—reward-hack activation identifies latent policy states, while entropy and decision-context features improve risk estimation for when exploitation becomes actionable.
AI.motivation: Safety monitoring in language-model agents is complex due to cycles of observation, reasoning, and action. Reward hacking poses a critical risk, and understanding how it manifests and can be detected/mitigated in agentic decision-making is necessary for safe deployment.
AI.method: Fine-tuned adapters on the School-of-Reward-Hacks dataset are applied to ReAct-style agents in Gameable ALFWorld and WebShop. Agents are instrumented with activation-based reward-hack scores, token-level entropy, and decision-context features. The study evaluates next-step prediction and activation-direction steering for risk estimation and mitigation.
AI.result: Adapters transfer reward-hack tendencies, especially when environments expose proxy-reward affordances. Reward-hack activation alone is insufficient for mitigation; entropy and context-calibrated features improve risk estimation. Activation-direction steering reduces proxy-exploit behavior in certain mixed-adapter regimes.
AI.conclusion: Context-calibrated internal monitoring is effective: reward-hack activation identifies a latent policy state, while entropy and decision context help determine when that state leads to risky actions, supporting safer agent behavior.

title: Closing the Loop on Latent Reasoning via Test-Time Reconstruction
summary: Recent work moves intermediate reasoning from natural-language traces into latent or cache-level representations to reduce token overhead and avoid a discrete communication bottleneck. However, this shift also removes a key advantage of textual reasoning: intermediate states are no longer inspectable, making it difficult to determine whether a latent state still preserves the constraints of the original query. As a result, latent reasoning typically operates in an open loop, where a latent state is produced and consumed without an input-anchored fidelity check. We propose ReLAT (Reconstruction-Guided Latent Reasoning At Test Time), a self-supervised test-time training method that closes this loop using the query itself as the reference. Our key observation is that if a latent state faithfully represents a query, the query should be recoverable from it; if the query cannot be recovered, the latent state has lost task-relevant information. ReLAT operationalizes this principle by constructing a differentiable Question -> Latent Thought -> Question cycle and optimizing query reconstruction loss through the latent thought before answer generation. This anchors opaque latent computation to the problem specification it is supposed to represent. Across mathematical reasoning, knowledge QA, and code generation benchmarks on the Qwen family, ReLAT consistently improves over single-model inference, text-based collaboration, open-loop latent collaboration, and alternative test-time training objectives. On Qwen3-8B, ReLAT raises AIME 2024 accuracy from 56.7% to 73.3%, a 16.6-point gain over the strongest open-loop latent baseline.

AI.tldr: ReLAT is a self-supervised test-time training method that uses query reconstruction loss to close the loop in latent reasoning, ensuring latent states preserve task-relevant information. It improves accuracy across math, QA, and code benchmarks, e.g., raising AIME 2024 accuracy from 56.7% to 73.3% on Qwen3-8B.
AI.motivation: Latent reasoning removes inspectability of intermediate states, making it hard to verify whether latent states preserve original query constraints, leading to open-loop operation without input-anchored fidelity checks.
AI.method: ReLAT constructs a differentiable Question → Latent Thought → Question cycle, optimizing query reconstruction loss through the latent state before answer generation, using the query itself as the reference for self-supervised training at test time.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over single-model inference, text-based collaboration, open-loop latent collaboration, and alternative test-time training objectives across math, QA, and code benchmarks. On Qwen3-8B, AIME 2024 accuracy rose from 56.7% to 73.3% (16.6-point gain over the strongest open-loop latent baseline).
AI.conclusion: Closing the loop via query reconstruction anchors opaque latent computation to the problem specification, effectively improving latent reasoning fidelity and downstream task performance.

title: RedKnot: Efficient Long-Context LLM Serving with Head-Aware KV Reuse and SegPagedAttention
summary:
As the input length of large language model (LLM) serving continues to grow, the KV cache has become a dominant bottleneck in AI infrastructure. It limits GPU memory capacity, serving concurrency, cache reuse, and distributed scalability. Several important problems, including position-independent KV cache, prefix KV cache compression, hot/cold KV cache separation, and distributed KV cache management, all depend on how the KV cache is represented and managed. However, existing serving systems largely rely on a monolithic KV cache abstraction, where the KV cache is treated as a homogeneous sequence of token-level memory blocks and managed with similar policies across attention heads and serving scenarios. We observe that KV cache utility is highly structured across KV heads: different heads exhibit different functional roles, attention distances, and runtime importance. Therefore, a full KV cache is not always necessary for every head, token range, or serving scenario.
  We present RedKnot, a head-aware KV cache management system for LLM serving. RedKnot breaks the conventional monolithic KV cache abstraction by decomposing the KV cache along KV heads, whose importance and effective attention ranges vary significantly across serving scenarios. This head-level decomposition turns the KV cache from a monolithic tensor abstraction into a structured memory object, enabling RedKnot to uniformly support position-independent KV reuse, prefix KV compression, hot/cold KV separation, and distributed KV placement while preserving output fidelity and improving resource efficiency, without requiring model retraining or fine-tuning. RedKnot establishes a new foundation for AI infrastructure by transforming the KV cache from a monolithic, passive runtime artifact into a dynamic, model-aware runtime substrate for scalable LLM serving.

AI.tldr: RedKnot is a head-aware KV cache management system that decomposes the monolithic KV cache along KV heads to enable structured memory management, supporting position-independent reuse, prefix compression, hot/cold separation, and distributed placement without model retraining.
AI.motivation: Growing input lengths in LLM serving make KV cache a critical bottleneck for GPU memory, concurrency, cache reuse, and scalability. Existing systems treat KV cache as a monolithic, homogeneous token-level sequence, ignoring that different KV heads exhibit distinct functional roles, attention distances, and runtime importance—making a full KV cache unnecessary for every head, token range, or scenario.
AI.method: RedKnot decomposes the KV cache along KV heads, creating a structured memory object instead of a monolithic tensor. This head-level decomposition captures varying importance and effective attention ranges across heads and serving scenarios, enabling unified support for multiple KV cache optimization techniques without retraining or fine-tuning.
AI.result: RedKnot uniformly supports position-independent KV reuse, prefix KV compression, hot/cold KV separation, and distributed KV placement while preserving output fidelity and improving resource efficiency.
AI.conclusion: RedKnot establishes a new infrastructure foundation by transforming the KV cache from a monolithic, passive runtime artifact into a dynamic, model-aware runtime substrate for scalable LLM serving.

title: ToolChoiceConfusion: Causal Minimal Tool Filtering for Reliable LLM Agents
summary:
Large language model agents increasingly rely on external tools, but larger tool menus can reduce reliability and efficiency by increasing wrong-tool calls, premature actions, and token cost. Existing tool-selection methods often optimize semantic relevance, exposing tools whose names or descriptions match the user request. We argue that relevance is insufficient: a tool may be related to the task while still being unnecessary or premature at the current step.
  We propose Causal Minimal Tool Filtering (CMTF), a training-free method that selects tools by causal sufficiency. CMTF uses lightweight precondition-effect contracts to expose only the minimal next-step tool frontier needed to advance from the current state toward the user goal. Across multi-step tool-use tasks, we compare CMTF with all-tools exposure, keyword retrieval, state-aware filtering, and causal-path ablations, measuring task success, wrong-tool calls, premature actions, tool exposure, and token cost. In the main benchmark with 102 tasks, 100 tools, four LLM backends, and 2448 task-method-model runs, CMTF matches the strongest causal baseline in aggregate success while reducing visible tools from 100 to one per step and reducing token usage by about 90% relative to all-tools exposure.

AI.tldr: CMTF is a training-free method that uses causal sufficiency and precondition-effect contracts to filter tools, reducing visible tools from 100 to 1 per step and token cost by ~90% while maintaining task success.
AI.motivation: Larger tool menus reduce reliability and efficiency due to wrong-tool calls, premature actions, and token cost. Existing relevance-based selection is insufficient because relevant tools may still be unnecessary or premature at the current step.
AI.method: CMTF (Causal Minimal Tool Filtering): a training-free method using lightweight precondition-effect contracts to select only the minimal next-step tool frontier based on causal sufficiency from the current state toward the user goal.
AI.result: Across 102 tasks, 100 tools, 4 LLM backends, and 2448 runs: CMTF matches the strongest causal baseline in aggregate success while reducing visible tools from 100 to 1 per step and reducing token usage by ~90% vs. all-tools exposure.
AI.conclusion: Relevance is insufficient for tool selection; causal sufficiency via precondition-effect contracts enables efficient, minimal tool exposure without sacrificing task success.

title: TRACE: A Temporal Conditional Estimation for Multimodal Time Series Foundation Models
comment: 5 figures and 5 tables in the main paper, plus appendix
summary: Time series foundation models (TS-FMs) aim to learn generalizable temporal representations that can be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks. In real-world multimodal settings, time series are frequently affected by temporal misalignment and partial modality missingness, where different modalities are observed at heterogeneous time scales or are partially absent. Existing approaches typically rely on naive imputation or masking strategies, which fail to account for cross-modal dependencies and often lead to misaligned or degraded representations. We propose TRACE, a conditional estimation paradigm for multimodal time series foundation model pipelines under missingness and irregular sampling, allowing incomplete target modalities to be systematically inferred from available auxiliary modalities. We evaluate TRACE on diverse multimodal benchmarks spanning healthcare and affective computing, including the MIMIC-IV clinical dataset and the CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI benchmarks for multimodal sentiment analysis. Across a range of downstream prediction tasks and missing-modality settings, TRACE consistently outperforms prior multimodal fusion approaches, demonstrating improved robustness to severe modality missingness and more reliable cross-modal representations.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a conditional estimation paradigm for multimodal time series foundation models that handles temporal misalignment and missing modalities by inferring incomplete target modalities from available auxiliary modalities, outperforming prior fusion approaches on healthcare and affective computing benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing TS-FMs rely on naive imputation or masking strategies that fail to account for cross-modal dependencies under temporal misalignment and partial modality missingness in real-world multimodal settings, leading to degraded representations.
AI.method: TRACE proposes a conditional estimation paradigm that systematically infers incomplete target modalities from available auxiliary modalities within multimodal time series foundation model pipelines, addressing missingness and irregular sampling.
AI.result: TRACE consistently outperforms prior multimodal fusion approaches across diverse downstream prediction tasks and missing-modality settings on MIMIC-IV, CMU-MOSI, and CMU-MOSEI benchmarks, demonstrating improved robustness to severe modality missingness and more reliable cross-modal representations.
AI.conclusion: Conditional estimation via available auxiliary modalities is an effective strategy for handling modality missingness and irregular sampling in multimodal time series, yielding robust cross-modal representations for downstream tasks.

title: Multi-ResNets for Subspace Preconditioning in Constrained Optimization
summary: We propose MResOpt, a staged residual neural network architecture for constrained optimization problems. Our architecture fits within predict-complete-correct pipelines and decomposes constraint satisfaction by priority through intermediate re-completion and stage-aware losses. The framework enables domain-informed ordered constraint satisfaction which allows the network to utilize ordinal structure when present. Under an idealized infinite-width regime, we show that our design behaves as sequential Gaussian Process regression. On synthetic QP, QCQP, and SOCP benchmarks, the staged architecture improves high-priority constraint satisfaction across convex and non-convex settings. On line-flow-constrained AC optimal power flow, we introduce a physics-motivated constraint ordering and show that MResOpt supports a learned division of labor that keeps iterates on the equality manifold, achieving substantially lower high-priority violation than reprojected baselines while remaining computationally efficient.

AI.tldr: MResOpt is a staged residual neural network for constrained optimization that decomposes constraint satisfaction by priority using intermediate re-completion and stage-aware losses. It behaves like sequential GP regression in infinite-width limit and outperforms baselines on QP, QCQP, SOCP, and AC optimal power flow benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing neural network approaches for constrained optimization often treat all constraints uniformly, failing to leverage ordinal priority structure. This leads to poor satisfaction of high-priority constraints, which is critical in real-world applications like power systems.
AI.method: MResOpt uses a staged residual architecture within a predict-complete-correct pipeline. It decomposes constraint satisfaction by priority through intermediate re-completion steps and stage-aware loss functions. The architecture can incorporate domain-informed ordering of constraints.
AI.result: On synthetic QP, QCQP, and SOCP benchmarks (convex and non-convex), the staged architecture improves high-priority constraint satisfaction. On AC optimal power flow with physics-motivated ordering, MResOpt achieves substantially lower high-priority violation than reprojected baselines while remaining computationally efficient.
AI.conclusion: MResOpt effectively leverages ordinal constraint structure via staged residual learning, achieving better high-priority constraint satisfaction. The infinite-width analysis connects the architecture to sequential GP regression, providing theoretical grounding.

title: AIS-Based Vessel Trajectory Prediction Using Memory-Augmented Neural Networks
summary: Accurate vessel trajectory prediction is essential for safe and efficient maritime operations, enabling collision avoidance and supporting route optimization. Although memory-augmented neural networks have recently shown strong performance in pedestrian and road-vehicle trajectory prediction by selectively retrieving relevant information from an external memory, their potential for vessel trajectory prediction remains underexplored. This paper presents an empirical investigation of memory-based trajectory prediction using Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. Experiments on data from the Gulf of Mexico and the New York Bight demonstrate consistent and substantial performance gains over a range of deep learning baselines that do not incorporate an external memory.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically investigates memory-augmented neural networks for vessel trajectory prediction using AIS data, showing substantial improvements over non-memory baselines across two maritime regions.
AI.motivation: Accurate vessel trajectory prediction is critical for maritime safety and efficiency (collision avoidance, route optimization). Memory-augmented networks have succeeded in pedestrian and road-vehicle prediction but their application to vessel trajectories remains unexplored.
AI.method: Empirical investigation of memory-based trajectory prediction using AIS data, comparing memory-augmented neural networks against deep learning baselines without external memory.
AI.result: Consistent and substantial performance gains over non-memory baselines on datasets from the Gulf of Mexico and the New York Bight.
AI.conclusion: Memory augmentation is effective for vessel trajectory prediction, bridging a gap between land-based and maritime trajectory forecasting.

title: LLM Self-Recognition: Steering and Retrieving Activation Signatures
comment: To appear in Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Recent advances in interpretability suggest that large language models (LLMs) implicitly encode signals in their generated text that enable self-recognition of their outputs. We demonstrate that this capability is reliable, even in low-entropy scenarios, and that it can be amplified through targeted intervention. By steering the internal residual stream during generation with a random sparse vector, we create a detectable fingerprint that enables attribution of a given text to a specific LLM. This signal is recoverable from the activations of an LLM used as a detector, achieving over 98% accuracy across multiple detection settings while preserving the quality of generated text. As AI-generated content proliferates, this approach offers a practical alternative to traditional detectors by leveraging the model's natural representation structure for attribution rather than embedding a signal externally. Our contributions include: (i) establishing reliable self-recognition capabilities in LLMs, (ii) a simple steering mechanism enabling multi-LLM identification with no quality degradation, (iii) demonstrating that activation spaces contain exploitable structure for encoding signals without semantic interference.

AI.tldr: LLMs encode self-recognition signals that can be amplified via random sparse vector steering of the residual stream, enabling >98% attribution accuracy across multiple detection settings without degrading text quality.
AI.motivation: As AI-generated content proliferates, there is a need for practical attribution methods that leverage models' natural representation structures rather than external signal embedding, offering an alternative to traditional detectors.
AI.method: Steering the internal residual stream during generation with a random sparse vector creates a detectable fingerprint; this signal is recovered from the activations of an LLM used as a detector.
AI.result: Achieves over 98% accuracy across multiple detection settings while preserving the quality of generated text.
AI.conclusion: Activation spaces contain exploitable structure for encoding signals without semantic interference, enabling multi-LLM identification with no quality degradation.

title: DragOn: A Benchmark and Dataset for Drag-Based GUI Interactions
summary: GUI agents - vision-based models that control desktops, web browsers, and mobile devices through graphical user interfaces - promise to automate a wide range of digital tasks. While million-scale datasets have enabled substantial progress on click-grounding, drag grounding (e.g. drag-and-drop, swipe, highlight) data remains an order of magnitude smaller and current models fall short on complex drag-based interactions. We introduce DragOn, a drag grounding benchmark and training dataset covering four domains: text highlighting, cell selection, element resizing and slider manipulation. The dataset comprises 286K training screenshots and 3.5M training tasks, plus a 2000-example held-out evaluation suite. We evaluate proprietary (GPT, Claude) and open-weight (Qwen, Kimi, Holo) models, as well as a Qwen VLM fine-tuned on our training data. Results suggest that our dataset could improve performance of state-of-the-art models on downstream computer-use tasks.

AI.tldr: DragOn is a benchmark and training dataset for drag grounding in GUI agents, covering four domains with 286K screenshots and 3.5M tasks, showing potential to improve state-of-the-art models on computer-use tasks.
AI.motivation: While click-grounding has advanced due to million-scale datasets, drag grounding (drag-and-drop, swipe, highlight) remains under-resourced with an order of magnitude less data, causing current models to underperform on complex drag-based interactions.
AI.method: The authors introduce DragOn, a drag grounding benchmark and training dataset covering four domains: text highlighting, cell selection, element resizing, and slider manipulation. It comprises 286K training screenshots and 3.5M training tasks, plus a 2000-example held-out evaluation suite.
AI.result: Proprietary (GPT, Claude) and open-weight (Qwen, Kimi, Holo) models were evaluated. A Qwen VLM fine-tuned on DragOn training data showed improved performance on downstream computer-use tasks.
AI.conclusion: The DragOn dataset could improve performance of state-of-the-art models on downstream computer-use tasks, particularly for drag-based interactions.

title: TokenMizer: Graph-Structured Session Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Context Management
comment: 12 pages, 10 figures. Code and benchmark available at https://github.com/Shweta-Mishra-ai/tokenmizer
summary: Large language model (LLM) deployments for long-horizon tasks face a fundamental constraint: context windows are finite while productive work sessions are not. When history exceeds the Maximum Effective Context Window (MECW), critical structured information - architectural decisions, task transitions, file histories - is silently discarded. Existing mitigations treat history as flat text, destroying the relational structure that makes sessions resumable. We present TokenMizer, an open-source proxy system that models LLM session history as a typed knowledge graph. The schema defines 14 node types and 7 edge types. A hybrid extraction pipeline populates the graph incrementally, while a three-tier checkpoint system serializes it into compact resume blocks. An 8-layer compression pipeline reduces context overhead, and a semantic cache reduces repeated-query latency. Evaluated on a controlled benchmark of 21 sessions spanning 5 domains, TokenMizer demonstrates significant token economy. It produces resume blocks averaging 78 tokens (range: 42-124) - 2x smaller than evaluated baselines (159-170 tokens) - while achieving higher decision recall (+9-17 percentage points). Crucially, baselines only preserve that a technology was mentioned; TokenMizer preserves the rationale. Across all sessions, TokenMizer achieves mean task recall 51.0%, decision recall 46.6%, and file recall 58.7%. Variance reflects domain heterogeneity: explicit imperative phrasing (software engineering) scores higher than implicit reasoning (research). Ablation studies show fuzzy label matching is the dominant improvement factor (+33 pp task recall). The heuristic compression achieves 47.3% token reduction with zero external dependencies. TokenMizer provides a queryable alternative to text-retention baselines at half the token cost.

AI.tldr: TokenMizer is an open-source proxy system that models LLM session history as a typed knowledge graph with 14 node types and 7 edge types, using a hybrid extraction pipeline and three-tier checkpoint system to produce compact resume blocks averaging 78 tokens (2x smaller than baselines) while achieving higher decision recall (+9-17 pp) across 21 sessions in 5 domains.
AI.motivation: LLM deployments for long-horizon tasks face a fundamental constraint: finite context windows versus unbounded productive work sessions. When history exceeds the Maximum Effective Context Window (MECW), critical structured information (architectural decisions, task transitions, file histories) is silently discarded. Existing mitigations treat history as flat text, destroying the relational structure that makes sessions resumable.
AI.method: TokenMizer models LLM session history as a typed knowledge graph (14 node types, 7 edge types). A hybrid extraction pipeline populates the graph incrementally. A three-tier checkpoint system serializes into compact resume blocks. An 8-layer compression pipeline reduces context overhead. A semantic cache reduces repeated-query latency. Fuzzy label matching is the dominant improvement factor.
AI.result: Evaluated on 21 sessions across 5 domains. Resume blocks average 78 tokens (range: 42-124) — 2x smaller than baselines (159-170 tokens). Higher decision recall (+9-17 pp). Mean task recall 51.0%, decision recall 46.6%, file recall 58.7%. Heuristic compression achieves 47.3% token reduction with zero external dependencies. Fuzzy label matching yields +33 pp task recall improvement.
AI.conclusion: TokenMizer provides a queryable alternative to text-retention baselines at half the token cost. Baselines only preserve that a technology was mentioned; TokenMizer preserves the rationale. Variance reflects domain heterogeneity (explicit imperative phrasing scores higher than implicit reasoning).

title: Boosting Brain-to-Image Decoding with TRIBE v2 Data Augmentation
summary: Brain decoding is limited by the availability of labeled neural data, and remains challenging in low-data regimes. To address this issue, we investigate whether and when brain decoding can be boosted by augmenting small fMRI datasets with synthetic data generated by a pretrained model of fMRI responses to stimuli. We use TRIBE v2, a large encoding model pretrained on more than 1000 hours of fMRI responses to video, audio and language. For each dataset, we evaluate systematic grids that show how the performance of image decoders varies with the amount of synthetic data used for training. Our results, based on two datasets (the 7T fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset and 3T fMRI BOLD5000), show up to 68% improvement in Top-10 image-retrieval accuracy compared to decoders trained only on real data. Importantly, the proportion of augmented data required to reach a given image decoding performance needs to be adjusted depending on the data source. Surprisingly, image decoders trained exclusively on synthetic fMRI can perform above chance in some settings, suggesting that TRIBE v2 can support zero-shot brain-to-image decoding. Together, these results show how large-scale models of the fMRI responses to sight, sound and language may provide a foundation to improve the data efficiency for image decoding.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether synthetic fMRI data generated by TRIBE v2 (a large pretrained encoding model) can augment small real fMRI datasets to improve brain decoding performance, achieving up to 68% improvement in Top-10 image-retrieval accuracy and even enabling zero-shot brain-to-image decoding.
AI.motivation: Brain decoding is limited by the scarcity of labeled neural data, making it challenging in low-data regimes. The authors aim to address this data efficiency problem by exploring whether synthetic fMRI data augmentation can boost decoding performance.
AI.method: The authors use TRIBE v2, a large encoding model pretrained on over 1000 hours of fMRI responses to video, audio, and language. They generate synthetic fMRI data to augment small real datasets and systematically evaluate grids showing how image decoder performance varies with the amount of synthetic data used for training. Experiments are conducted on two datasets: 7T fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset and 3T fMRI BOLD5000.
AI.result: Up to 68% improvement in Top-10 image-retrieval accuracy compared to decoders trained only on real data. The optimal proportion of augmented data depends on the data source. Image decoders trained exclusively on synthetic fMRI can perform above chance in some settings, demonstrating zero-shot brain-to-image decoding capability.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale models of fMRI responses to sight, sound, and language (like TRIBE v2) can serve as a foundation to improve data efficiency for image decoding, suggesting synthetic data augmentation is a viable strategy for overcoming limited labeled neural data in brain decoding.

title: Where Should Knowledge Enter? A Layered Framework for Knowledge Infusion in Multimodal Iterative Generative Mo
summary: Multimodal generative models produce fluent outputs but remain unreliable when generation must respect structured, domain-specific, or safety-critical knowledge. Existing methods incorporate knowledge through mechanisms such as prompt augmentation, guidance, latent editing, or fine-tuning, yet they are typically categorized by technique rather than by the component of the generative process they modify. We argue that knowledge infusion in iterative generative models is fundamentally anintervention-layer problem. Since thegenerative process unfolds as a trajectory of internal states, knowledge can act on four structurally distinct components of this process: the input/output boundary, the transition function, the intermediate state, and the model parameters. This maps to four intervention layers: surface, trajectory, latent, and parametric infusion. We instantiate the framework in diffusion models, map representative methods to all four layers, and derive design principles for multi-layer composition. In a controlled safety-alignment experiment using a multimodal knowledge graph with two diffusion backbones, we implement three of the four layers cumulatively, surface (input-side and output-side) and trajectory--latent (mid-generation). We show empirically that each additional layer addresses failure classes that prior layers cannot reach, reducing knowledge-violating outputs by 70.97% compared to vanilla generation and empirically confirming the framework's complementarity prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that knowledge infusion in iterative generative models is fundamentally an intervention-layer problem, identifying four structurally distinct layers (surface, trajectory, latent, parametric) mapped onto the generative trajectory (input/output boundary, transition function, intermediate state, model parameters). Empirical validation in a safety-alignment experiment with diffusion models shows cumulative multi-layer intervention reduces knowledge-violating outputs by 70.97%.
AI.motivation: Multimodal generative models produce fluent outputs but remain unreliable when generation must respect structured, domain-specific, or safety-critical knowledge. Existing methods categorize knowledge infusion by technique rather than by which component of the generative process they modify, lacking a unified structural understanding.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework treating knowledge infusion as an intervention-layer problem, identifying four layers: surface (input/output boundary), trajectory (transition function), latent (intermediate state), and parametric (model parameters). They instantiate the framework in diffusion models and conduct a controlled safety-alignment experiment using a multimodal knowledge graph with two diffusion backbones, implementing three layers cumulatively.
AI.result: Each additional layer addresses failure classes that prior layers cannot reach. Cumulative multi-layer intervention reduces knowledge-violating outputs by 70.97% compared to vanilla generation, empirically confirming the framework's complementarity prediction.
AI.conclusion: The intervention-layer framework provides a principled way to categorize and compose knowledge infusion methods in iterative generative models. Multi-layer composition is complementary and effective for improving reliability in safety-critical domains.

title: An Infectious Disease Spread Simulation Based on Large Language Model Decision Making
summary: Modelling individual decision-making during infectious disease outbreaks is crucial for understanding behavioural dynamics and informing effective public health interventions. Prior work has shown that large language models can simulate realistic human behaviour by generating agent decisions based on demographic prompts and situational context. We build on this foundation with a spatially grounded, agent-based simulation framework that integrates LLM-generated decisions about self-reported influenza-like illness into a census-based synthetic population of agents. Location is treated as a central feature: agents are assigned to spatial units within cities, capturing the spatial distributions of different demographic groups using real-world census data and enabling geographically diverse behavioural modelling. We implement and compare three decision scenarios, independent reasoning, household influence, and message framing, and simulate self-reporting outcomes in San Francisco and Atlanta. Results reveal that income and education are the dominant drivers of reporting rate variation, with smaller but consistent effects from geography, LLM model choice, and message framing. Our framework generates synthetic data that captures both social and geographic heterogeneity, supporting spatial epidemiological modelling and bias-aware behavioural analysis.

AI.tldr: A spatially grounded, agent-based simulation framework using LLM-generated decisions and real census data to model self-reported influenza-like illness behavior in San Francisco and Atlanta, finding income and education as dominant drivers of reporting variation.
AI.motivation: Understanding individual decision-making during infectious disease outbreaks is crucial for effective public health interventions, and prior work has shown LLMs can simulate realistic human behavior, motivating the extension to spatially explicit frameworks.
AI.method: Integrates LLM-generated decisions about self-reported influenza-like illness into a census-based synthetic population of agents with spatial assignments, comparing three decision scenarios: independent reasoning, household influence, and message framing.
AI.result: Income and education are the dominant drivers of reporting rate variation; smaller but consistent effects from geography, LLM model choice, and message framing are observed.
AI.conclusion: The framework generates synthetic data capturing both social and geographic heterogeneity, supporting spatial epidemiological modeling and bias-aware behavioral analysis.

title: Rethinking Infrastructure Inspection as Image Difference Classification: A Traffic Sign Case Study
comment: CVPR 2026 Computer Vision for the Built World Workshop (CV4AEC @ CVPR)
summary: Digital twins (DTs) allow the digitalization of road infrastructure inspection, though this is hindered by limited annotated data. This work exploits the relational nature of continuous asset condition monitoring to reformulate image-based defect detection as image difference classification (IDC) to reduce data reliance. This was evaluated in a case study on low-resource traffic sign inspection with different IDC classifiers using a newly-curated, high quality dataset. Results indicate that the instruction-based classifier outperforms encoder-based ones and gains from comparison with reference images. This shows that IDC can be an effective task modeling for tackling data constraints in infrastructure inspection and DT asset condition updating.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Image Difference Classification (IDC) as a reformulation of defect detection to reduce data reliance for digital twin infrastructure inspection, demonstrating that instruction-based classifiers outperform encoder-based ones in low-resource traffic sign inspection.
AI.motivation: Digital twins enable digitalization of road infrastructure inspection but are hindered by limited annotated data for defect detection.
AI.method: Reformulates image-based defect detection as Image Difference Classification (IDC) by exploiting the relational nature of continuous asset condition monitoring; evaluated instruction-based and encoder-based classifiers on a newly-curated dataset for traffic sign inspection.
AI.result: Instruction-based classifier outperforms encoder-based classifiers and benefits from comparison with reference images.
AI.conclusion: IDC is an effective task modeling approach for tackling data constraints in infrastructure inspection and DT asset condition updating.

title: Humans' ALMANAC: A Human Collaboration Dataset of Action-Level Mental Model Annotations for Agent Collaboration
summary: Recent advances in LLM agents have enabled complex cognitive capabilities, such as multi-step reasoning, planning, and tool use, that increasingly position these agents as human collaborators. Effective collaboration, however, requires collaborators to continuously maintain and align mental models of their own reasoning,partners' intentions, and shared goals during the collaborative process. Today's agents rarely develop such capabilities since they are primarily optimized for task completion, and the community lacks authentic human collaboration data with action-level mental model annotations that could guide agents toward process-level collaborative competence. To bridge this gap, we present ALMANAC, a dataset of Action-Level Mental model ANnotations for Agent Collaboration built from the Map Task, a classic dyadic routing task from social science. ALMANAC contains 2,987 collaboration actions, each paired with theory-informed mental model annotations that record the participants' self-reasoning, perceived partner intent, and perceived team goal. We benchmark six LLMs on predicting humans' next-turn behavior and mental models. Our results demonstrate ALMANAC's utility in evaluating models' ability to simulate human collaborative behaviors and infer their underlying mental models.

AI.tldr: ALMANAC is a dataset of 2,987 collaboration actions with mental model annotations (self-reasoning, partner intent, team goal) from the Map Task, used to benchmark LLMs on predicting human collaborative behaviors and inferring mental models.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents lack collaborative competence because they are optimized for task completion rather than process-level collaboration, and there is no authentic human collaboration data with action-level mental model annotations to guide their development.
AI.method: The authors built ALMANAC from the Map Task (dyadic routing task), annotating 2,987 collaboration actions with theory-informed mental model annotations (self-reasoning, perceived partner intent, perceived team goal), then benchmarked six LLMs on predicting next-turn behavior and mental models.
AI.result: The dataset enables evaluation of LLMs' ability to simulate human collaborative behaviors and infer underlying mental models, demonstrating ALMANAC's utility as a benchmark.
AI.conclusion: ALMANAC bridges the gap in action-level mental model annotations for human collaboration, providing a resource to develop and evaluate agents with collaborative competence beyond task completion.

title: Risk Assessment of Autonomous Driving: Integrating Technical Failures, Ethical Dilemmas, and Policy Frameworks
summary: Autonomous driving technology has the potential to reduce the large number of road traffic accidents caused by human error each year, but it also brings new types of risks that need to be evaluated from the aspects of technology, ethics and regulations. Based on public crash data from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), disengagement reports from the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV), the MIT Moral Machines dataset, and a comparative regulatory analysis of five jurisdictions, we have found that the main types of technical failure modes are perception and classification errors. These account for a relatively large proportion of the reported accidents, and it can be concluded that there are different ethical frameworks for autonomous vehicle decision-making, and inconsistent regulations in different areas increase the uncertainty of widespread application. Generally speaking, the problems of technology, ethics and regulation are closely related and need to be solved together. Therefore, this paper recommends a more adaptive and cooperative governance approach that combines engineering standards, ethical discussion, and institutional supervision.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes autonomous driving risks from technical, ethical, and regulatory perspectives using NHTSA crash data, California DMV disengagement reports, MIT Moral Machines dataset, and comparative regulatory analysis across five jurisdictions. It identifies perception/classification errors as primary technical failures, highlights conflicting ethical frameworks, and notes regulatory inconsistencies. It recommends an adaptive, cooperative governance approach combining engineering standards, ethical discussion, and institutional supervision.
AI.motivation: Autonomous driving technology promises to reduce human-error-related accidents but introduces new types of risks. These multifaceted risks—spanning technology, ethics, and regulation—need systematic evaluation to inform safe and responsible deployment.
AI.method: The study draws on NHTSA public crash data, California DMV disengagement reports, the MIT Moral Machines dataset, and a comparative regulatory analysis of five jurisdictions to identify and characterize risks across technical, ethical, and regulatory dimensions.
AI.result: Perception and classification errors are the dominant technical failure modes in reported accidents. There exist divergent ethical frameworks for autonomous vehicle decision-making, and inconsistent regulations across jurisdictions amplify uncertainty for widespread deployment.
AI.conclusion: Technical, ethical, and regulatory issues are closely intertwined and must be addressed jointly. The paper recommends a more adaptive and cooperative governance approach integrating engineering standards, ethical discussion, and institutional supervision.

title: Unsupervised Skill Discovery for Agentic Data Analysis
summary: Inference-time skill augmentation provides a lightweight way to improve data-analytic agents by injecting reusable procedural knowledge without updating model parameters. However, discovering effective skills for data analysis remains challenging, as reliable supervision is expensive and success criteria vary across analytical formats. This raises the key question of how to discover reusable data-analysis skills from unlabeled exploration alone. We propose DataCOPE, an unsupervised verifier-guided skill discovery framework for data-analytic agents. DataCOPE derives verifier signals from the exploration trajectories and uses them to characterize relative quality or aggreement among trajectories. It iteratively coordinates a Data-Analytic Agent for trajectory generation, an Unsupervised Verifier for signal extraction, and a Skill Manager for contrastive skill distillation. For report-style analysis, we instantiate the verifier as an Adaptive Checklist Verifier that derives task-specific criteria, scores reports by verifiable coverage, and iteratively refines the checklist. For reasoning-style analysis, we instantiate it as an Answer Agreement Verifier that groups trajectories by answer agreement and uses self-consistency as an auxiliary signal. We evaluate DataCOPE on report-style analysis from Deep Data Research and reasoning-style analysis from DABStep. Across both settings, DataCOPE consistently improves held-out performance over baselines. Averaged across four model settings, DataCOPE improves the mean score by 9.71% and 32.30% on report-style and reasoning-style tasks respectively.

AI.tldr: DataCOPE is an unsupervised verifier-guided framework that discovers reusable data-analysis skills from unlabeled exploration trajectories, improving held-out performance by 9.71% on report-style tasks and 32.30% on reasoning-style tasks across four model settings.
AI.motivation: Inference-time skill augmentation improves data-analytic agents without parameter updates, but discovering effective skills is challenging due to expensive supervision and varying success criteria across analytical formats. The key question is how to discover reusable data-analysis skills from unlabeled exploration alone.
AI.method: DataCOPE uses an unsupervised verifier to derive signals from exploration trajectories, characterizing relative quality or agreement. It iteratively coordinates three components: a Data-Analytic Agent (trajectory generation), an Unsupervised Verifier (signal extraction), and a Skill Manager (contrastive skill distillation). Two verifier instantiations are proposed: Adaptive Checklist Verifier (report-style) and Answer Agreement Verifier (reasoning-style).
AI.result: On Deep Data Research (report-style) and DABStep (reasoning-style), DataCOPE consistently improves held-out performance over baselines. Averaged across four model settings, it improves mean score by 9.71% on report-style tasks and 32.30% on reasoning-style tasks.
AI.conclusion: DataCOPE demonstrates that unsupervised verifier-guided skill discovery is effective for data-analytic agents across different analytical formats, providing a lightweight way to improve performance without labeled data or parameter updates.

title: Agent Memory: Characterization and System Implications of Stateful Long-Horizon Workloads
summary: LLM agents are increasingly deployed on long-horizon tasks requiring sustained reasoning over extended interaction histories. Realizing this at scale requires agents to persistently store, retrieve, and update their own memory across sessions. A rich ecosystem of agent memory systems has emerged spanning flat retrieval, LLM-mediated extraction, consolidating fact stores, and agentic control flows. Yet, their system-level behavior remains uncharacterized. We present the first systems characterization of agent memory. First, we introduce a system-oriented taxonomy classifying agent memory systems along four axes. Second, we build a phase-aware profiling harness attributing cost to construction, retrieval, and generation. Third, we characterize ten representative systems across two benchmark suites, uncovering how design choices shift cost across the write and read paths. Finally, we derive 10 system recommendations covering construction scheduling, capability floors, amortization via query volume, freshness-latency tradeoffs, and fleet-scale management.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systems characterization of LLM agent memory, introducing a taxonomy, profiling harness, and empirical analysis of ten representative memory systems, deriving ten actionable design recommendations.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly deployed on long-horizon tasks requiring sustained reasoning over extended interaction histories, yet the system-level behavior of agent memory systems remains uncharacterized, creating a gap in understanding how design choices impact performance and cost.
AI.method: The authors develop a system-oriented taxonomy classifying agent memory along four axes, build a phase-aware profiling harness that attributes cost to construction, retrieval, and generation phases, and characterize ten representative systems across two benchmark suites.
AI.result: The analysis uncovers how design choices shift cost across write and read paths in agent memory systems, revealing tradeoffs between construction scheduling, capability floors, amortization via query volume, freshness-latency tradeoffs, and fleet-scale management.
AI.conclusion: The paper derives 10 system recommendations covering key aspects of agent memory system design such as construction scheduling, capability floors, amortization strategies, freshness-latency tradeoffs, and fleet-scale management.

title: Vortex: Efficient and Programmable Sparse Attention Serving for AI Agents
summary: Sparse attention is becoming increasingly important for serving large language models (LLMs) as generation lengths continue to grow. However, deploying and evaluating new sparse attention algorithms at scale remains highly engineering-intensive, slowing both human researchers and AI agents in exploring the sparse attention design. To address this challenge, we present Vortex, a system that combines a Python-embedded frontend language atop a page-centric tensor abstraction for expressing a broad range of sparse attention algorithms, with an efficient backend tightly integrated into modern LLM serving stacks. Vortex enables rapid prototyping, deployment, and evaluation of sparse attention algorithms, effectively translating their theoretical efficiency gains into real-world throughput improvements. As a result, Vortex substantially accelerates the design and iteration of sparse attention algorithms. First, AI agents use Vortex to automatically generate and refine diverse algorithms, the best reaching up to $3.46\times$ higher throughput than full attention while preserving accuracy. Second, Vortex extends sparse attention to emerging architectures and very large models that are otherwise hard to experiment with, reaching up to $4.7\times$ higher throughput on the MLA-based GLM-4.7-Flash and $1.37\times$ on the 229B-parameter MiniMax-M2.7 on NVIDIA B200 GPUs.

AI.tldr: Vortex is a system with a Python-embedded frontend and page-centric tensor abstraction for rapidly prototyping, deploying, and evaluating sparse attention algorithms in LLMs, achieving up to 4.7× throughput gains over full attention on large models.
AI.motivation: Deploying and evaluating new sparse attention algorithms at scale is highly engineering-intensive, slowing both human researchers and AI agents in exploring the sparse attention design space.
AI.method: Vortex combines a Python-embedded frontend language with a page-centric tensor abstraction for expressing sparse attention algorithms, paired with an efficient backend integrated into modern LLM serving stacks.
AI.result: AI agents using Vortex generated algorithms reaching up to 3.46× higher throughput than full attention; Vortex achieved up to 4.7× higher throughput on MLA-based GLM-4.7-Flash and 1.37× on the 229B-parameter MiniMax-M2.7 on NVIDIA B200 GPUs.
AI.conclusion: Vortex substantially accelerates the design and iteration of sparse attention algorithms, effectively translating theoretical efficiency gains into real-world throughput improvements across diverse architectures and very large models.

title: Benchmark Everything Everywhere All at Once
summary: Benchmarks are fundamental for evaluating and advancing LLMs and MLLMs by providing standardized and explicit measures of performance. However, their construction is labor-intensive and hard to reuse, raising concerns about sustainability and scalability. Moreover, existing benchmarks often quickly reach performance saturation after their release, resulting in insufficient discrimination among state-of-the-art models. To address these challenges, we introduce Benchmark Agent, a fully autonomous agentic system designed for benchmark building. Our framework orchestrates the complete benchmark construction pipeline, from user query analysis and subtask design to data annotation and quality control. To assess Benchmark Agent, we implement it to produce 15 representative benchmarks, spanning diverse evaluation scenarios, including text understanding, multimodal understanding, and domain-specific reasoning. Extensive experiments, including human evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge assessment, and consistency checks, demonstrate Benchmark Agent can generate high-quality benchmark samples with minimal human involvement. More importantly, through continual evaluation, we observe several insightful findings, including that current models struggle with certain domain-specific reasoning tasks. We believe that rapidly evolving benchmarks can contribute significantly to the research community. The preview and code will be publicly available at the demo page and code repository.

AI.tldr: Benchmark Agent is an autonomous system for constructing LLM/MLLM evaluation benchmarks that reduces human labor, produces high-quality samples, and reveals ongoing model limitations in domain-specific reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Current benchmark construction is labor-intensive, hard to reuse, and quickly reaches performance saturation, making it unsustainable and insufficient for discriminating among state-of-the-art models.
AI.method: A fully autonomous agentic system that orchestrates the complete benchmark construction pipeline — from user query analysis and subtask design to data annotation and quality control — producing 15 benchmarks covering text understanding, multimodal understanding, and domain-specific reasoning.
AI.result: Human evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge assessment, and consistency checks show that Benchmark Agent generates high-quality benchmark samples with minimal human involvement. Continual evaluation reveals that current models still struggle with certain domain-specific reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: Rapidly evolving benchmarks enabled by autonomous agentic systems can contribute significantly to the research community by addressing sustainability and discrimination challenges in model evaluation.

title: Goedel-Architect: Streamlining Formal Theorem Proving with Blueprint Generation and Refinement
summary: We introduce Goedel-Architect, an agentic framework for formal theorem proving in Lean 4 centered on blueprint generation and refinement. A blueprint is a dependency graph of definitions and lemmas that builds up to the main theorem. First, Goedel-Architect generates a blueprint of formally stated definitions and lemmas, along with declared dependencies. This blueprint is optionally guided by a natural language proof. Then, a tool-equipped Lean prover component closes each open lemma node in parallel using relevant dependencies. Failed lemmas in turn drive refinement of the global blueprint. This strategy contrasts with other mainstream approaches which use recursive lemma decomposition, and can inefficiently loop on dead-end strategies. Using the open-weight DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B-A13B) as the backbone, Goedel-Architect attains 99.2% pass@1 on MiniF2F-test and 75.6% pass@1 on PutnamBench. With an optional natural-language proof seeding the initial blueprint on the harder problems, we additionally close the remaining two MiniF2F-test problems (reaching 100%), lift PutnamBench to 88.8% (597/672), and solve 4/6 on IMO 2025, 11/12 on Putnam 2025, and 3/6 on USAMO 2026. This represents state-of-the-art performance for an open-source pipeline at a price point up to 500x less than comparable open-source pipelines.

AI.tldr: Goedel-Architect is an agentic framework for formal theorem proving in Lean 4 that generates and refines a blueprint (dependency graph) of lemmas, achieves state-of-the-art results on MiniF2F-test (99.2% pass@1, 100% with seeding), PutnamBench (75.6%, 88.8% with seeding), and multiple competition problems, at up to 500x lower cost than comparable open-source pipelines.
AI.motivation: Existing formal theorem proving approaches use recursive lemma decomposition, which can inefficiently loop on dead-end strategies. The authors aim to design a more efficient, parallelizable framework that uses global blueprint generation and iterative refinement guided by failed proofs.
AI.method: Goedel-Architect first generates a blueprint (dependency graph) of formally stated definitions/lemmas, optionally guided by a natural language proof. Then a tool-equipped Lean prover component closes each open lemma node in parallel using relevant dependencies. Failed lemmas drive refinement of the global blueprint.
AI.result: Using DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B-A13B), achieves 99.2% pass@1 on MiniF2F-test and 75.6% on PutnamBench. With natural-language seeding: 100% on MiniF2F-test, 88.8% on PutnamBench, 4/6 on IMO 2025, 11/12 on Putnam 2025, 3/6 on USAMO 2026. State-of-the-art for open-source pipelines at up to 500x less cost.
AI.conclusion: Blueprint generation and refinement is an effective and cost-efficient strategy for formal theorem proving, outperforming recursive decomposition approaches and achieving state-of-the-art results among open-source pipelines.

title: MLEvolve: A Self-Evolving Framework for Automated Machine Learning Algorithm Discovery
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly applied to long-horizon tasks such as scientific discovery and machine learning engineering (MLE), where sustained self-evolution becomes a key capability. However, existing MLE agents suffer from inter-branch information isolation, memoryless search, and lack of hierarchical control, which together hinder long-horizon optimization. We present MLEvolve, an LLM-based self-evolving multi-agent framework for end-to-end machine learning algorithm discovery. By extending tree search to Progressive MCGS, MLEvolve enables cross-branch information flow through graph-based reference edges and gradually shifts the search from broad exploration to focused exploitation with an entropy-inspired progressive schedule. To allow the agent to evolve with accumulated experience, we introduce Retrospective Memory, which combines a cold-start domain knowledge base with a dynamic global memory for task-specific experience retrieval and reuse. For stable long-horizon iteration, we further decouple strategic planning from code generation with adaptive coding modes. Evaluation on MLE-Bench shows that MLEvolve achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple dimensions including average medal rate and valid submission rate under a 12-hour budget (half the standard runtime). Moreover, MLEvolve also outperforms specialized algorithm discovery methods including AlphaEvolve on mathematical algorithm optimization tasks, demonstrating strong cross-domain generalization. Our code is available at https://github.com/InternScience/MLEvolve.

AI.tldr: MLEvolve is a self-evolving multi-agent framework for long-horizon ML algorithm discovery that uses Progressive MCGS (graph-based tree search with cross-branch information flow), Retrospective Memory (cold-start knowledge base + dynamic global memory), and decoupled strategic planning from code generation. It achieves SOTA on MLE-Bench and outperforms AlphaEvolve on mathematical algorithm optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing MLE agents suffer from inter-branch information isolation, memoryless search, and lack of hierarchical control, which hinder sustained self-evolution in long-horizon tasks like scientific discovery and ML engineering.
AI.method: 1) Progressive MCGS: graph-based tree search extending MCGS with cross-branch reference edges and entropy-inspired progressive schedule for exploration-to-exploitation transition. 2) Retrospective Memory: cold-start domain knowledge base + dynamic global memory for experience retrieval/reuse. 3) Decoupled strategic planning from code generation with adaptive coding modes.
AI.result: SOTA on MLE-Bench across average medal rate and valid submission rate under 12-hour budget (half standard runtime). Outperforms AlphaEvolve on mathematical algorithm optimization tasks, showing cross-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: MLEvolve effectively addresses key limitations of existing MLE agents through structured search, memory mechanisms, and hierarchical control, achieving strong performance in long-horizon self-evolving ML algorithm discovery.
